their memory and to rejoice with them since they arc now in our Father' s house ,
where there is " no more death, neither ~orrow nor crying ." Whatever our creed
or faith . we must sound a note of gladness . not because they have passed from
among us. but because they are now living in the presence of the great triune
God, the Supreme Architect of the Uni verse.
The Greeks held that death was the greatest gift to man from the gods, an<l the
naturalness of death was expressed by the great Buddha when he said. "as all
eanhen vessels made by the potter end in being broken, so is the life of mortals."

It's people like you who make Him "SO REAL"
My God is no stranger. He's friendly and gay . ..
And He doesn't ask me to weep when I pray .
It seems that I pass Him so often each day
In the faces of people I meet on my way . ..
He 's the star~ in the heaven , a smile on some face .
A leaf on a tree or a rose in a vase ...
He's winter and autumn and summer and spring ...
In short, GOD IS EVERY REAL, WONDERFUL THING .
I wish I might meet Him much more than I do ,
I would if there were MORE PEOPLE LIKE YOU .
Brethren: this is our assignment.

" Man comes an<l tills the soil and lies beneath. " There , in one short sentence.
the poet Wordswo rth told the story of life and death, and short indeed is our
allotted span in this world. We, the living, who are gathered here today know
that "a time will come and the wisest know not how soon, when all distinction
save that of goodness shall cease, and, death. the mighty leveler of human
greatness, reduce us to the same state . "
The Grand Lodge of Masons of California is an institution. but those who
compose it are monal. and one by o ne , year after year, these mortals must obey
the solemn summons and depa!i to the realms beyond the skies. while other
workmen from the quarries come forward to take their places and to carry on
their works .
"They are pass ing away, these dear old friend s.
Like leaves on the current cast;
With never a break in the rapid flow,
We watch them as one by one they go
Into the solemn past."
The roll of the deceased in an organization with the number of members of this
Grand Lodge is inevitably long. Time does not permit more than a few eulogies
of our departed brothers. yet all are wonhy . Their individual names will be
inscribed in the printed record of our Annual Communication.
During the past year four hundred fift y-six (456) of our Past Masters . Masters
and Wardens were translated from this imperfect to that all perfect. glorious and
celestial Lodge above where the Supreme Grand Master of the Uni verse forever
presides. Three hundred three (303) of our Lodges suffered losses. One Lodge
lost six (6); another Lodge lost fi ve (5); four Lodges lost four (4 ) each;
twenty-eight Lodges, three (3) each; seventy-six Lodges. two (2) each; and one
hundred ninety-three Lodges lost one (l) each .
Among the departed was our well known and beloved Past Grand Master
Elmer Wilson Heald who was called to the Supreme Lodge on high on November
26, 1975. "Elmer" as he was affectionately known was truly a dedicated Mason.
The eulogy for Brother Heald will be given by a very good and close personal
friend , the Rev. Dr . Robert B. Watts, P.M .. former Grand Chaplain and Grand
Orator.

Mine is the treasured privilege of speaking briefly to this Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge concerning the life of its 98th Most Worshipful Grand Master- Elmer Wilson Heald. a distinguished jurist and Ma.~onic Leader am.I our
beloved friend of many year~. Judge Heald. known to hi~ legion of friends
simply as ·'Elmer'·. was born in Marshall County, Kamas. on January 7', 1885.
Corning to California. he attended public schools in Santa Cruz and Palo Alto.
Following a periou of teaching in Idaho. he returned to California and received
his Doctor of Jurisprudence Degree at Stanford School of Law.
In the broad branches of Freemasonry. \fost Worshipful Brother Heald's
willingness to devote great portions of hi' time anu talent to teaching anu
administering. and the great skill with which he performed those functions.
carried him to the very pinnacles of honor anu to the highe.-.t stations of
comrnanu.
He became a Master Mason in El Centro Lodge No.38..t in 1920. and served as
its Master in l 9..i3 anu again in 19..i 7. In 1960. Judge Heald WU!> elected Junior
Grand Warden. and in 1963-at the n:markabk age of 78-was installed as Most
Worshipful Grand Master of this Granu Lodge.
Nor were his Masonic Offices and honors restricted to the Blue Lodge. He \\as
a past commander of the Imperial Valley Commander} of the York Rite. and
held the rank and distinction of an honorary lmpector General of the 33rd Degree
of the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry for the Southern Juri~diction of the United
States. But to all who have known him, and they are countless in number~. our
Mo st Worshipful -Brother·_, life speaks of far more than honors. numerous a~ they
have been.
Note the hrcadth and sweep of his interests and accomplishments. A graduate
of the Stanford Law School, as has been said, he turned, not to the eqabli~hcd
law firms of the cities. hut to the then pioneering area of Imperial County. It was
there that he became. through the years of friendship anu service which followed.
the true patriarch of the Valley.
Always intensely devoted to his Country, our Brother served a~ an officer in
two wars. first as a Lieutenant anu later as a Lieutenant Colonel. Anu that
devotion to plain. honest Americanism never left him.
It lay behind his successful battles with the radical I. W.W. which vainly
attempted to invade the Valley. It motivateu a lifetime of devotion to the young
men and women whom he encouraged in their youth grnurs. And it hrought him
the overwhelming support of his whole county as he wa~ repeatedly returned tn
the high post of Ju Lige of the Superior Court. a post which he relinquished only to
ass ume the duties of Granu ~\faster of our Craft.
But to look hehinu these achievements, we find the rare spirit of one who, with
great mouesty and complete disregard of personal preferment. sought to he a
frienu to all who passed his way. His door ,,.,·a~ al way~ open to those in need or
perplexity. Hi~ skills were ever ready to aid in the solution of community

ORGANIZATION

Christian Brothers High School in Sacramento on May 16. 1976. Thi ~ ~chool.
which stresses training youth from relatively poor homes for careers in trades
following graduation, is supported by the public at large and highly regarded by
all who are acquainted with it. Our participatio n did much for the image of
Masonry.
For the first time in fi ve years a new Lodge . Fountain Valley Bicentennial
Lodge . U.D . . was instituted on the evening of August 20. 1976. What a thrill for
your Grand Maste r to perform this ce remony and to know that the enthusiasm.
fine leadership and young members hip are bound to result in a fine. successful
addition to the Lodges of our Jurisdiction.
An additional thrill was afforded your Grand Master by the opportunity to
institute a second Lodge. Daylight Bicentennial Lodge. U.D .• on September 24.
1976. This Lodge in Sacramento will fill a great need in the area. enabling night
workers and others to attend Lodge during the daytime .
One other unusual event was the dedication of the rebuilding of Quitman
Lodge No. 88 in the Malakoff Diggings State Historic Park on August 23. 1976.
A beautiful bronze plaque is to be placed on the building so that all who vis it this
most interesting State Park will know that Masonry had an important part of
"winning the West." On this project your Grand Master was faced with an
emergent decision . Masons had the choice early in the year to participate in
rebuilding the interior part of the :-econd floor of the building which is to house
Quitman Lodge or to lose forever the opportunity to have the Lodge included in
the structure as it was during its hey day. Five thousand dollars were needed for
materials. The project is top on the list for re~tomtion of Ma~onic Hi sto rical

APPROVAL OF EMERGENT D ECISION
To EXPEND $5 ,000 FOR THE R E BUILDING OF
Q UITMAN LODGE NO. 88 TEMPLE

The Committee 011 Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Maste r seeks Grand Lodge approval of hi s dec ision to permit five
thousand dollars to be provided for the rebuilding of the Quitman Lodge No. 88
Temple at Malakoff Diggings State Historic Park in Nevada County . His
decision was emergent because of time restraints imposed by lhe State Division
of Parks and Recreation. which agency is in charge of the restoration program of
the old mining community of North Bloomfield, the community originally served
by Quitman Lodge. In actuality the expenditure o f 1hese Grand Lodge funds
supplemented the considerable contribution of materials and labor provided by
Maso ns in the area, particularly by members of the Lodges in the 208th Masonic
District.
In 1974. this Grand Lodge adopted a policy and procedure s relative to Grand
Lodge part icipalion in the acqui sition. restor.ition and preservation of significant
and important Maso nic histo rical sites. The prescribed procedure invo lved
submiss ion of a proposed project to lhe Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic
History for their determination as to appropriateness for Grand Lodge participation. following which the proposal is to be reviewed and approved by bot h the
C ommittee on Finance and the Committee o n Po licy and General Purposes, with
final dec ision to be made by vote of the Grand Lodge. It is unfortunate that the
time restraints pre viously referred to prevented application of this procedure in
this instance.
Your Committee o n Policy and General Purposes believes that the Grand
Master's action in this emergent matter was in the best interest of the Grand
Lodge of California and that the restoration of this o ld and typical early
California Masonic Temple will bring great credit to our Fraternity. as well as
furnishing much in the way of public education respecting the institution of
Freemasonry.
However. your Committee also be lie ves that in accorda nce with the policy and
procedure adopted in 1974. and to complete the record. the Quitman Lodge
project should be referred to the Committee on Masonic Histo ry for their
post-action review and anticipated e ndorsement . Further. your Committee expresses the hope that future projec ts having to do with Grand Lodge participat ion
will be of such a nature as to not prevent the full application of the adopted Grand
Lodge policy and procedure .
I move approval of the Grand Master's deci sion and the suggested referral to
the Committee on Masonic History, and your Committee on Polic y and General
Purposes recommends a " Yes" vote.
Adopted.

THE LODGE

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Recommendati on No . I results from the Grand Master's interpretation of the
word "nominal " a~ used in re lation to the value of an award fo r the winner of a
Public Schoo l essay contest. The Grand Master, recogn iz ing that inflat ion ha!>
made a previo us designation of .. nominal" as $25 .00 o r less to be now
something less than nominal. and in recogniti on of the variation between Lodge~
as to their financial capabilities. has recom me nded that tbe amount of award!>
such as the one for a Public Schools essay contest be "well within the financial
capabilities of the Lodge. "
The committee be lieves that the underlying philosophy whi ch gave use to the
adoption of the language "nominal value" to still be valid . We. too . recognize
the fact of inflation and we also recognize that what may be " nominal " to o ne
Lodge is not necessarily · ·nominal'' to another . Ho we ver, we arc concerned w ith
the latitude which is suggested by the Grand Master's recomme nd ation . Seriou~
que stions could ari se suc h as, "Who is to determine what is 'well within the
financial capability of a Lodge?' Is capability to be judged upon re!>ources at
hand, or monies expected to be acquired?" And so on.
While the deci sion and recommendati on of prior Grand M asters. approved by
Grand Lodge, are aids and guides to current Grand Masters , they are often based
upo n a particular factual circumstance and may not necessarily be control I ing on
subsequent Grand Masters.
As seen by the .events giving rise to this resolution, the practical problem of
naming a specific amount to be "nominal" is a rec urrent o ne. It is doubtful that
the new criteria suggested by the resolution would solve the problem .
Therefore. we suggest that rather than changing the concept of what is
"nominal" that lhe G rand Lodge should give consideration to establishing
~ui~elines to aid everyone concerned in the ap plication of the principle of
hm1ting awards to a "nominal value."
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes therefo re reco mmends that
this recommendation of the Grand Master, No. I , not be adopted .
The Grand Maste r's recommendation was adopted .

R ECOMMENOATION (3)
G RAN D M ASTER 'S DECISI ONS VALID 0NL Y FOR H!S Y EA R

The CommitTee on Policy and Genaal Purposes:
In the Grand Master·~ message he has made a recommendat ion directed to the

California Ma~onic Code and panicularly to Grand Maste r' s Decisions . The
recommendat ion is that any decision made by a Grand Master shall only remai n
valid during his year in o ffice.
Your Com mi ttee on Policy and Gene ral Purposes believes that to auopt this
recommendat ion would truly defeat the intent and purpose of our Masonic Code.
Our Juri sdic tion is and ha~ bee n since 1850 governed by a Co nstitution an<l
Ordinances. These have been re printed from time to time and. of course. have
been amended throughout t he years.
At the present time . our Constitution and Ordinances arc co ntained in the
California Maso nic Code. Second Edition. 1975. These are printed in black ink .
The Annotatio ns. printed in brown ink , are only interpretation s by a particular
Grand Master. Committee on Jurisprudence or Committee on Policy a nd Gene ral
Purpose. The interpretation s o r Annotations arc only d irccted to a specific
situation which is no t specifically identified by the Constitution or Ordinances.
These Annotations are not the law: the Constitution and Ordinances arc the
Jaw. In some cases over the years. some of these Annotations or rulings ha ve
become so basic that upon revision of th e Masoni c Code, they have been placed
in the basic law . In other cases Resolutions ha ve been proposed which include a
basic Annotation as a pan of our law.
The procedure outlined above is basic to our re publican fonn of government
and fo llowed by this Grand Lodge for 126 years. These proced ure s assure us the
flexibility of government by the governed .
To expun ge arbitrarily a Grand Master's decision or recommenda tion approved by Grand Lodge. arri ved at after much consulta tion and deliberation.
would be a step backward. If chat Annotation is helpful in the future as a
guideline for the individual Lodges , Inspectors and a future Grand Master. it
should remain . It. of course, is not controlling on a future Grand Master, unl ess
appropriate amendmenh are made to our basic law and approved by 5/ 6's vote of
Grand Lodge .
1 move the adoption of Recommenda tion No. 3 but. your Committee on Polic y
and General Purposes reco mme nd~ a ·· No'· vote.
Not Adopted.

RECOMMEND ATION (5)

50 YEAR PIN 50 YEARS FROM DATE OF R AISING

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This recommenda tion would enable a Master Mason to receive a 50 year pin
afte r only 47 years of service. The present regulation (Sec . 2436 of the California
Masonic Code) states :
' ' In computing the length of time requisite for issuance of a 50 year o r 75 year
button , periods during which the Brother held a dimit or was suspended fo r
non-payment of dues must be add ed to t ime when sa id Brother wo uld
otherwise have been elig ible to receive such award, proyided. however, that
the period between the issuance of a dimit for the purpose of becoming a
Charter Member of a ne w Lodge and the institution of the new Lodge is not an
interruption of the req uired number of years of continuo us membership ."
Your Committee believes the present regulation retains the concept of requiring 50 years of ser vice for an honor award and incorporates a necessa ry
safeguard .
I move the adoption of Recommendatio n No. 5 and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

PROCLAMATION
PUBLIC SCHOOLS MONTH - APRIL 1976
"PUBLIC SCHOOLS - OUR FUTURE"
Fifty-six years have passed into history since the late Charles
Albert Adams, during his term as Grand Master of Masons in California
and Hawaii, took a crucial step in halting the deterioration of our
Public Schools by proclaiming PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK throughout the
jurisdiction, thus enlisting the Masons of California and Hawaii in
the struggle against forces that were destroying our system of Public
Education.
The years have smiled on our efforts. The record shows that the
downward trend was soon reversed, thereby allowing our Public Schools
to reassume their rightful role in the preservation of our liberties
by educating our youth to become responsible citizens and by building
America's leaders of tomorrow.
The continued effectiveness of our Public Schools depends on our
unceasing support of this vital institution. It is appropriate right
now - in the patriotic atmosphere of America's Bicentennial - that we
rededicate ourselves wholeheartedly to the task of supporting and
strengthening.our system of Public Education.
Secure in the knowledge that I can count on the cooperation and
support of all good Masons, I now therefore proclaim the month of
April 1976 to be PUBLIC SCHOOLS MONTH throughout California and
Hawaii. I earnestly request that diligent effort be made to contact
every school district in this jurisdiction and arrange for a mutually
acceptable week in April for an appropriate Public Schools Observance,
and that all constituant Lodges actively promote and participate in
this annual event.
In furtherance of this objective, I direct that no Lodge programs
or meetings be held during the designated week for purposes other than
Public Schools Observances, ~ith the exception of Stated Meetingsr and
That this Proclamation, where feasible, be published in Lodge bulletins ' together with other pertinent Public Schools Week publicity: and
That this Proclamation be read at the March and April Stated
Meetings of all.Lodges.
Dated:

January 20, 1976
sincerely and ~t~rn~lyf}.

Vand Master

PROCLAMATION
PROCLAMATION

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

YOUTH ACTIVITIES WEEK
March 14-21, 1976
This Bicentennial Year of Our Great Country marks the
fifty-fifth year of DeMolay in California. This well-established organization, Job's Daughters and Rainbow for Girls
are all actively promoting Masonry's highest ideals among
our youth.
They need and deserve our support, our prayers and our
encouragement. Let us not fail them, for these moral
intelligent and patriotic young people are soon desti~ed to
carry forward not only the ideals of Masonry but especially
the great heritage of our country.
I therefore proclaim the week of March 14-21 1976 to
be Youth Activities Week. During that period all Masons are
urged to show how important we consider our youth organizations
to ~e. Visit their meetings. Assist in their projects.
Invite them to exemplify their work in your Lodge. Let them
know that we care.
1

Please read this Proclamation at the Stated Meetings of
each Lodge in March and, if convenient, send a copy to each
member of the Lodge through your bulletin or otherwise.
Dated: February 10, 1976

The true happiness we have is that we share with others, and
no virtue is greater than that of sharing - the precious
gift of charity. Each degree in Masonry teaches that lesson,
and the Holy Scriptures provide us with countless examples
of charity as guides for abundant living.
Our greatest Masonic charity in California is for our Homes
in Covina and Decoto. The residents there are our charges,
and we wish for them the best care that we can provide.
Rising costs of that service and depreciated money are taking their toll in meeting our obligations to the children
at Covina and the elderly at Decoto. Outside cases for
relief also are substantially increasing the need for funds.
At the present time we have collected only about half the
amount we need if we are to top last year's contributions
in excess of one million dollars. Our task is great, but
we can meet ~he challenge if each of us will help. Now is
the time to act.
I, therefore, proclaim the month of May 1976 to be
Masonic Homes Endowment Month
and request that this proclamation be read at the April and
May Stated Meetings of all Lodges in California and Hawaii.
Wherever practicable, send a copy of this proclamation to
~
each member of the Lodge.
Da<od,

Maroh 10, 1976

PROCLAMATION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

In this Bicentennial Year we have been learning much
of the sacrifice of labor, blood and treasure that our
~orefathers made to establish a government deriving its
JUSt ~owe:s from the consent of the governed under our
Constitution.. To preserve the freedoms won with such
difficul~y.requi:es us to b~ exemplary in the discharge
of our civil duties and to inspire our youth to pass them
along to future generations. To this end knowledge and
respect for our Constitution are essential.
I ther~for~ declare the month of September, 1976
to be Constitution Observance Month and direct every
Lodg~ i~ this Jurisdict~on to participate in an appropriate
patriotic observance, either in connection with a Bicentennial observance or other event. Such observance should be
open to the public at large and stress the value of our
freedoms and our responsibility to preserve them.
I further direct that this proclamation be read at
the.August and Se~tember Stated Meetings and where convenient, to be printed in Lodge bulletins for September, 1976.
Dated:

June 17, 1976

!ff::.:~.;-.

On this occasion the Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibility of
reporting to the Brethren ofJhe Grand Lodge concerning the financial condition
of the Grand Lodge and its entities.
In the main, the financial figures and comments thereon by the Grand
Treasurer are based upon the official audit statement of Lindquist, Von Husen
and Joyce, Certified Public Accounts for each <;>fthe following Masonic entities:
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
The Masonic Homes of California
The California Masonic Memorial Temple
The California Masonic Foundation
The period of the audit covered the year ending June 30, 1976 and contains a
record of revenue and expense for the fiscal year. These official audit statements
are on file in the Grand Secretary's office and may be inspected there. Your
Grand Treasurer attests that all are in proper form and as stated by Lindquist,
Von Husen and Joyce, were made in accordance with generally accepted
accounting practices.
On June 30, 1976, the sum of $61,152,894 in cash and securities, at cost,
belonging to the Grand Lodge of California and its entities were under the
jurisdiction of your Grand Treasurer. In addition, other assets, including real
estate and notes receivable, amounted to $17,079,967. The total of all assets at
June 30, 1976 was $78,232,861. That total ten years ago was $39,093,983. All
of our securities are deposited in the vaults of the Crocker Bank, 1 Montgomery
Street, San Francisco, Ca. 94104. Unannounced, on the 20th day of July 1976,
your Grand Treastkr, with two representatives from the Grand Lodge Accounting Department, together with two accountants from the firm of Lindquist, Von
Husen and Joyce, our certified public accountants, called at the Crocker Bank
and entered the vaults where a physical check of our securities verified that all
were safely deposited. The bank official in charge of the vault operation was
Brother Walter R. Brosalme, a member of Parnassus Presidio Lodge Number
388.

THE GRAND LoDGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Grand Lodge of California as can be determined by an analysis of the
audited statement of the Grand Lodge Account indicates an excess of expense
over revenue of $77,470. The marketable securities in the fund are valued at
79. 7% of cost. Of course there is no realized loss until the securities are sold. In
the statement of appropriations the Grand Master approved supplemental expenditures of $64,375 some of which are non-recurring.
To the end that better controls be provided in our financial affairs, your Grand
Treasurer recommends that no funds in excess of the budgeted amounts authorized by this Grand Lodge, be paid out, unless approved by the Committee on
Finance and/or authorized by the Grand Master.

In reporting on the financial statements of the Masonic Homes of California,
you are advised the Endowment Fund balance at June 30, 1976 was $35,446,85 9
an increase of $3,527 , 757 over last year. Only the earnings of this fund may be
used to support the Homes. Great tribute must be paid to the Masonic Homes
Endowment Committee whose continuing outstanding efforts have once again
been instrumental in providing one million dollars in contributions. The balance
of funds were from memorials, grants, wills and bequests. As your Grand
Treasurer has stated in the past, funds available to the Masonic Homes in
unrestricted use enables the Homes Board to determine critical or urgent
priorities for the use of such funds. Your Grand Treasurer again urges the
Brethren of the Grand Lodge to encourage donations, grants or other giving to be
on an unrestricted basis whenever possible. This is particularly true now, when
substantial funds will be needed to pay for the improvements scheduled for our
outstanding Masonic Home at Union City. The Reserves and General Fund
balance of the Masonic Homes stands net at $23,224,472 at June 30, 1976, a
gain of $3 ,480,493 for the current year.
Because of what we considered to be an over-assessment on the lands owned
by the Home adjacent to our buildings, your Grand Treasurer met with officials
from the Alameda County Assessor's Office . Conferences at their office and also
at the Home property in Union City, resulted in a reduction in the assessed value
of the property not used for the physical plant of the Home. The assessment was
reduced from $431,700 to $297,000, a total reduction of $134,700. Further
reductions are being sought by application to the Appeals Board. Lodges in our
Jurisdiction are urged to inform successful petitioners that $25.00 of their
initiation fee is contributed to a charitable agency , namely the Masonic Homes
and is thus tax deductible.
Since the inception of the Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund , your. Grand
Treasurer has continued to make numerous trips to various areas of California to
ascertain property valuations on real estate proposed to be deeded to the Masonic
Homes. The Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund, initiated and guided by
Edward H. Siems our Grand Secretary, is now a successful economic addition to
the Masonic Homes. The efforts, knowledge and skill of Ed Siems on behalf of
this program is matched only by his energy and never-ending love for the
Fraternity.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

I am pleased to submit to this Grand Lodge, pursuant to Masonic Law, my
sixteenth Annual Report. The office of Grand Secretary canies with it the related
duties of Secretary for the Masonic Homes of California, the California Masonic
Memorial Temple Corporation, the California Masonic Foundation, the California Masonic Retirement Plan and the Investment Committee as well as certain
other committees of Grand Lodge.
Your Grand Lodge Office Staff is responsible for the records pertaining to the
various entities of Grand Lodge. All financial records, and supporting papers,
vouchers and books for each of the entities are on file in the Grand Lodge Office.
The Chairman and members of the Finance Committee, as required by
Masonic law, have reviewed details of disbursements made by Grand Lodge
during the year.
The Grand Treasurer's Report records all monies received and credited to the
accounts under his name and custody.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

INVESTMENT LIST OF GRAND LODGE
AND ALL ENTITlES

Committeemen, who are close to the workings of the Grand Lodge office and
to whom we have presented the preliminary plans, have suggested that we
move forward with the project. We have an estimate of approximately
$140,000 to $150,000 to do the remodelling in two stages and still be able to
carry on the daily office work. The reconstruction time estimate is approximately six months. If we could move out of the present work space, the
architect estimates it would take about half the time or three months.
Consideration is being given to the possibilities of occupying space in two or
more committee rooms on "G" Floor. This should result in a substantial
savings in time and money.

Each year we have reproduced the list of investments in the Grand Treasurer's
Report and in the Annual Proceedings. The list is substantial . The cost of paper
and printing continues to increase. We now have a continuing inventory of all
investments on the computer. Our investment advisor furnishes quarterly printouts of the entire list. The list in the Proceedings is at least six months out of date
by the time the Proceedings are distributed, since investments are recorded as of
the fiscal year closing. Copies of our Investment Portfolio may be reviewed by
any member of Grand Lodge in the Grand Secretary's Office . With these new
developments it has been determined that the lists should not be reproduced in the
printed reports. The Staff has accepted that determination.

We are placing the matter of the proposed reconstruction of the Third Floor
before the members of Grand Lodge so that it can be referred to the proper
committees for ultimate recommendation and the decision of Grand Lodge.

GRAND LOOOE OFFICE

In 1958, when we first occupied the Grand Lodge Office in the Memorial
Temple, we had a total of nine employees. This number was supplemented with
extra help prior to and during each Annual Communication.
With the increased demands on personnel by committees and government
(city, state and federal reports, etc.), our Staff, of necessity, has been increased.
All employees are on the Grand Lodge payroll with the exception of two Homes
Investigators, who work exclusively for Masonic Homes of California. Periodically time studies are made, and the time worked by employees to handle these
demands is allocated and charged back to the various Masonic entities.
With the increased number of employees studies have been made on a
rearrangement of the Office to provide more adequate working space for each
employee. Our employee Lunch Room is too small, and our general office for
stenographers, clerks and others is no longer adequate under the present circumstances.
The following recommendation has been presented to the Finance Committee,
the Past Grand Masters and the Elective Grand Lodge Officers:
In order to eliminate noise from the computer it is proposed that it be housed
in a separate room with accompanying cabinets and record desks . The view
terrace outside the Grand Secretary's Office be eliminated, and the Grand
Secretary's Office and the Assistant Grand Secretary's Office be located in the
space now occupied by the terrace. Most of the interior walls be removed,
which would necessitate moving the Conference Room into the area now used
as Masonic Homes offices. The new plan includes a large employees lunch
room-namely, the office currently assigned to the Assistant Grand Secretary.
We believe by removing certain walls, improving the lighting, using glass
partitions for special offices, installing sound absoming portable partitions and
carpeting on the floor throughout the work area, that a modem office can be
developed to house our entire Staff in a more comfortable and efficient
manner. Personnel is the key to an efficient office. We owe it to them to see
that the physical requirements a1..:: met.
Although the cost of remodelling will be substantial, it will be paid out of
reserves and not out of per capita tax money. Grand Lodge Officers and

Personnel
Our Office Staff is loyal and are dedicated to conscientously serving this
Grand Lodge and its several entities with continued enthusiasm.
At the time this report is drafted, all but one of our Staff is healthy and on the
job. I must report, however, that the year 1976 was a difficult year from the
standpoint of health. Early in January our Chief Accounting Officer was
hospitalized until June 19, 1976. She is back on the job, and the doctor assures us
she is well on the road to complete recovery. In addition three other Staff
members required hospitalization and are now back on the job. One other
member did not return after hospitalization. We are indeed grateful that the future
looks much brighter, but our Blue Cross coverage has been taxed to the limit.
However, I am pleased to report that prior to January 1, 1976, we enjoyed a
rather substantial reserve which will offset some of the potential increased
premium.
CONSOLIDATION OF LoDGES

We continue to process paper work on consolidation of Lodges. In 1964 we
had a total of 711 Lodges. Due to consolidations we are now down to 670, which
figure includes two Lodges recently instituted under dispensation. The usual
reasons for consolidations are generally declining interest, small attendance, and
lack of officer material. There must be other compelling reasons for the lack of
leadership, since this is not a universal experience. We have many Lodges that
are active, growing and carrying on a full and adequate program with men hoping
for an opportunity to serve as officers. We have two groups petitioning for
dispensations to form Lodges.
It is encouraging to see that our Deputy Grand Master has decided to appoint a
special committee to be called Lodge Resources Development for the singular
purpose of assistance to ailing Lodges. Hopefully they will be able to suggest
some corrective measures resulting in fewer consolidations which, in most
instances, is not the answer to their problems. It is sincerely hoped that the Lodge
Resources Development Committee in working with ailing Lodges will find the
answer.

54

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
ACCOUNTING RECORDS

Increasing demands for additional detail continue to result in needed expansion
of our computer operation. The line-printer, reported as being on order in my last
year's report, has been installed and is performing efficiently. It has speeded up
the process of statistical accounting materially. We are pleased with its performance.
On recommendation of our progressive Elective Line Officers our Staff is
making a detailed and in-depth study to find out if it is feasible to add
sophistication to our computer operation. Consideration will be given to adding
certain membership information which will be more readily available for reference or analysis. Advantages would result to the Elective Grand Lodge Officers
in making committee appointments and to the Fraternity as a whole, pointing out
the direction of its growth, its strengths and its weaknesses. Of necessity the
proposed development must progress in stages and the results expected will not
become effective immediately.
APPRECIATION

Speaking for our Staff we wish to express our sincere appreciation for the
leadership of the Most Worshipful Grand Master, John F. Roberts, Jr., and for
the complete cooperation of the Elective Line Officers. Each of them has given
inspiration to all Masons qf this Grand Jurisdiction. We are indeed deeply
grateful for all of their assistance and support.
I could not close this report without acknowledging that the Grand Secretary's
Staff works as a unit to serve Grand Lodge. My personal thanks to each member
for their continued dedication.

Referred to Committee on Distribution.

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee once again calls to the attention of Lodge Secretaries that
many of the applications for dispensation to hold an election at other than the
stated time failed to certify that the requesting Lodge had complied with the
requirements of Section 2502 of the California Masonic Code, particularly the
requirement that two-thirds of the members present at a Stated Meeting voted to
request a dispensation.
The Committee finds that the Grand Master has acted properly in granting or
denying the applications for dispensations and in approving Life Membership
Resolutions and we recommend that this action be approved.
Respectfully submitted,
LEO E. ANDERSON, Chairman

In the past, your Committee on By-Laws has called the attention of the Lodges
of this jurisdiction to the need to have a realistic amount authorized for
expenditure by the Charity Committee of the 'Lodge between Stated Meetings.
This remains an important item of consideration as is the recommendation that
care taken in specifically identifying legal holidays by name when designating
exceptions to the regular date of the Stated Meetings of a Lodge. For a review of
this Committee's concern in regard to these matters, we would refer the members
of this Grand Lodge and the constituent Lodges to the Report of this Committee
as set forth in the 1974 Proceedings of this Grand Lodge. We suggest that these
recommendations be reread and due consideration given thereto.
. Your Committee also recommends that careful and thoughtful consideration be
given to the comments of Edward H. Siems, P.G.M., our Grand Secretary, as
contained in his article entitled "Are We Placing Enough Value On Our
Product?" appearing on Page 103 of the Summer 1976 issue of the "California
Freemason" (Volume 23, No. 3). That article discusses the question of the effect
of inflation upon the dues payable for membership in the Masonic Fraternity.
It is to be noted that soine ten years ago, in 1966, the average dues for Lodges
in this jurisdiction was $17.38 with some 300 constituent Lodges charging less
than that average.
In the ten years from 1966 to 1975 there have been some 619 amendments to
By-Laws increasing dues, plus the 78 occurring in 1976.
. A reference to the 1975 Proceedings and the Grand Secretary's Report
discloses that as of 1975 the average dues had increased to $20.57. As of that
time, the number of Lodges with dues less than the $17 .38 referred to above had
shrunk to a mere 133 with inflation still at work reducing that number.
It is important also to note that the minimum dues of $12.00 has not been
changed since 1953 and only 25 Lodges last year were able to retain that
minimum for their members. When one considers the increase in the cost of
living and the decrease in the value of the dollar since 1953, it is surprising, only,
that even those 25 Lodges can exist on the minimum dues.
This Committee feels that the time has arrived for a careful review to be made
of our present dues structure and it is recommended that the Committee on
By-Laws appointed for the new Masonic year be instructed to work with the
Grand Secretary in conducting a study of the basic financial needs of Lodges and
to report its findings with appropriate recommendations at the Annual Communication in 1977.
~s usual, the Grand Secretary and his staff have provided efficient and diligent
assistance to both the constituent Lodges and to this Committee. We extend our
thanks to Brother Siems and his associates for their help which has greatly
simplified our work, and we encourage Lodges contemplating changes to their
By-Laws to take advantage of this dedicated and knowledgeable group of people
by securing from them the necessary forms and instructions to accomplish the
desired changes. They can make your work much simpler.
Most Worshipful, I move the acceptance of this report, the approval of the
amendments referred to in Exhibit B of the Report of the Grand Secretary
together with the additions referred to herein.

Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Trial Review:
There have been referred to your Committee on Trial Review since the 1975
Communication, twenty-five Trial Records, of which one is a petition for

TRIAL RECORD No. 2072
An Entered Apprentice Mason in Oroville Lodge No. 103 was charged with
un-Masonic conduct in two specifications, the record being devoid of any
evidence at the first charge, that he filed a false "missing persons" report with
the Sheriff of Butte County relative to the disapperance of his wife.
The second specification alleged that the accused pleaded guilty to a criminal
charge of involuntary manslaughter in connection with the death of his wife after
having been charged with first degree murder.
Involuntary manslaughter is not per se a crime consisting of moral turpitude
but the Trial Master erroneously accepted the admission by the accused of the
plea and conviction as sufficient evidence upon which to base his finding of guilt
and determined the penalty to be suspension.
The record is otherwise silent as to the facts giving rise to the charge, other

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2077
This is a case involving 3 separate failures by a member of Whittier Lodge No.
323 to honor his commitment as a Master Mason to tell the truth. He pied guilty
to all three charges "with an explanation" to each, but no explanation was ever
offered.
The accused was raised on October 24, 1974. Contrary to his promise in
Question 15 not to apply for or receive any degree or to be initiated in an
organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master
Mason until he has passed a proficiency examination in the 3rd Degree, and in no
event within 12 m9nths after receiving the Degree of Master Mason, the accused
did by petition dated February IO, 1975, three and one-half months after he was
raised, ask for admission to that organization. This application was received by
the Scottish Rite on March 3, 1975.
On April 22, 1975, just six months after receiving his 3rd Degree, while being
interrogated by a personnel committee of the Scottish Rite, he stated he had been
raised in January 1973, a date 22 months prior to the actual event.
Further, on February 14, 1975, 3 weeks prior to the time his petition for the
Scottish Rite was actually received by that organization, he petitioned Al
Malaikah Shrine Temple for membership and was made a member of that
organization on May 31, 1975, seven months after being raised.
Based on the guilty pleas, the Trial Master made a finding of guilt on all three
charges and fixed the penalty at suspension.
Masonry is built on the integrity of its members. A Mason's word must be his
bond, particularly with his fellow Masons. In light of the aggravated nature of the
offenses committed in the case, and in order to promote uniformity of punishment throughout the Jurisdiction for the same offense, your Committee on Trial
Review presents the following resolution and recommends its adoption:
RESOLVED, that the findings of guilt in Trial Record No. 2077 be approved
but that the penalty be raised to expulsion, and the member expelled from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2078
The Accused, a Member of Stockton Lodge No. 498, was charged in the
United States District Court for the Eastern District of California with twentythree (23) counts of uttering forged United States Savings Bonds being a
violation of Title 18 USC Section 495, a felony. He was charged with having
taken certain forged United States Savings Bonds, which he received from a third
party, and which had already been endorsed out of his presence, to a bank where
he requested they be cashed and falsely represented to the bank clerk that they
belonged to his aunt and uncle.
The accused was found Guilty of all 23 counts of the offense charged by a jury
in the aforementioned Court. On February 4, 1975, the accused was sentenced to
imprisonment for a period of five (5) years, to be confined in a jail-type
institution for a period of ninety (90) days. Sentence to run concurrent on all 23
counts. The balance of the sentence was suspended and the accused was placed
on probation for a period of five (5) years on the special condition that he make
restitution in the amount of Five Thousand ($5,000.00) Dollars.
Charges of un-Masonic conduct were filed against the accused alleging two
specifications:
One that, he negotiated for sale 23 forged bonds and misappropriated the funds
therefrom; and two, that he did stand trial and was convicted of "uttering
Forged United States Savings Bonds as charged in the indictment."
He was tried by Stockton Lodge No. 498 and found not guilty on each
specification by that Lodge.
Your Trial Review Committee has carefully examined the Trial Record and
Transcript of the Trial, some 56 pages in length. The record indicates ample
evidence that the accused should have known something was amiss respecting
the manner in which he received the Bonds and the request that he. cash them.
There also appears to be sufficient uncontradicted evidence !Pat/the accused
himself knowingly gave false information to the bank clerk who cashed the bonds
at his request, which clearly establishes his knowledge of wrong doing.
Your Trial Review Committee unanimously determined that it was clear from
the evidence presented at trial that he had committed the offense charged. and
that the finding of Not Guilty by the Commission was incorrect and resulted in a
Miscarriage of Justice.
We therefore, offer the following Resolution and recommend its adoption:
RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Commission in Record No. 2078
be reversed, the Accused be found guilty, the penalty be set at expulsion and that
the member be expelled from all rights and priveleges of Masonry.

ing of the requirement to present competent evidence; and because no evidence
was presented, the Commissioners acquitted the accused. After investigation it is
apparent to this Committee that evidence bearing on the charge is available; and
the charge being such a gravely serious one, it was a gross violation of Masonic
law for the Lodge to fail in its obligation to bring the facts before the
Commissioners.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the judgment of acquittal be reversed and the matter be
returned for retrial on competent evidence or on a sustainable showing of the
unavailability of such evidence.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2086
The accused, a member in good standing of Callayomi Lodge No. 282, was
charged with un-Masonic conduct in that he, on or about October 4, 1975, did
disrobe himself before Masons, their ladies and the public.
The accusers are members of Clear Lake Lodge No. 183 and Hartley Lodge
No. 199 respectively. The Master of Callayomi Lodge in his trial report has
accepted the written statements of the accusers, perhaps justly so, but has made
no indication in his report that he sought or found corroborating evidence of the
conduct allegedly occurring.
Section 3328 of the California Masonic Code requires a charge to be set forth
with clearness and precision and demands specification of the necessary particulars . Further, Section 3340, C.M .C. requires the Trial Master to personally make
a complete investigation where no response is made by the accused to the
accusation. The Trial Record is without evidence of the Trial Master's findings.
Absent in his findings there is insufficient evidence upon which to base a
recommendation to affirm.
We therefore move the adoption of the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that Trial Record No. 2086 be returned to the Trial Master and
that he be instructed to augment the record with a statement of his findings and
the results of his investigation.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER

Division 6 at Long Beach in February-Conducted by Ernest M. Newton.
Division 3 at Los Gatos in March-Conducted by Ulysess G. Patropulos.
Division l at Santa Rosa in April-Conducted by Burton 0. Young.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The relentless passage of time brings nearer and nearer the end of the 1976
Grand Lodge year, and in its lengthening shadows, I rise in compliance with the
requirements of my office to render unto this Grand Lodge a full and detailed
account of my services during the year, and to set forth therein a report of the
condition of the Lodges within this Grand Jurisdiction .
This report shall of necessity be a condensed one . However, I shall endeavour
to cover very thoroughly those areas of major concern where changes have
occurred or where problems of any magnitude exist. Those areas are: Ritual,
Lodge Administration, Leadership Training, Masonic Education and Officer
·
Procurement.
I am pleased to report some very significant advances in the areas of Ritual,
Masonic Education and Leadership Training ... New lines of communication
have been established, and they are now being utilized in our continuing war
against apathy.
Turning first to Ritual, it is of interest to note that it is in this area where the
greatest advances have been made this year .. . The many hours spent working
with the Ritual have proven to be very productive as we continue our quest for
total uniformity of the Ritual within the California Jurisdiction . It is most
gratifying to observe, that with a possible few exceptions, every Masonic Officer
in this Jurisdiction is not only well informed, but completely dedicated to a goal
of complete conformity to the California Adopted Ritual. Many areas of
disagreement have been resolved this year, and a few minor adjustments in the
work have brought it even nearer to its pure adopted form. Most of the credit for
progress in this area must be given those six magnificant Masons who serve as
both the left and right arms of the Grand Lecturer- The Six Assistant Grand
Lecturers; Masonic Ritual Experts who recognize no boundaries, nor do they
spare any effort in planning, teaching, assisting and instructing the Brethren
within their various spheres of influence. They are indeed the finest minds in
California Masonry and they give freely of their time and talents to provide the
type of Masonic Leadership which has established California Ritual as number
one among the Jurisdictions of the world. This Grand Lodge owes a great debt of
gratitude to all six of these Assistant Grand Lecturers who serve Masonry so well
from year to year.
To those thousands of Lodge Officers, Coaches and Past Masters who teach
and exemplify the Ritual as now taught by the Grand Lecturer, we commend you
for your efforts , and for your contribution toward uniform Ritual. To the few
who persist in "doing it their own way," we extend a cordial invitation for you
to "Join the Grand Lodge of California, and do it the right way."
Schools of Ritual Instruction were held this year at regular intervals, and at
various places throughout the State. The Ritual Committee held eight meetings
this year, and the Assistant Grand Lecturers conducted Divisional Schools for the
Inspectors of each Division on the average of eight times within the twelve month
period .. .. Inspectors' Spring conference sessions were held in the various
Divisions as follows:

Division 5 at Los Angeles in May-Conducted by George W. Perkins.
Division 4 at Fresno in June-Conducted by Vernon L. Gordon.
Division 2 at Sacramento in June-Conducted by Edward E. Seagle
At each of those Spring Conferences the Inspectors of the Division exemplified the Ritual of the Three degrees, and I am pleased to report that with only
minor exceptions, there was complete agreement on all points of Ritual throughout the entire State.
It was also our very great honor to· have had in attendance at all six of the
Inspectors' Conferences, the Grand Master and all members of the Elective
Grand Lodge Line . The Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master and the Grand
Secretary each had the opportunity to address the Inspectors at the Conferences,
and to brief them on plans for the future .
The present level of Ritual proficiency within the State leads me to conclude
that the absence of the Grand Lecturer's school of instruction for the Inspectors at
each Annual Communication has not in any way proven detrimental to our
system of Ritual instruction .
INSPECTORS

I continue to marvel at the amazing capacity of our Masonic Inspectors. They
teach, they counsel, they plan, they assist. To the Masters and the Lodges they
are friend, mentor, father confessor and leader. They are equally at ease
presenting the Gntnd Master, or instructing junior Officers in Lodge duties, and
to a man they are highly respected by those over whom they have been
appointed. They are reluctant to use the word "no," but they quite freely utilize
the word, "we." They are indeed the reason for Masonry's success in California, and I am extremely proud of them all.
The rate of turnover in the Inspectoral Corps has been rather high in 1976. In
the past twelve months, 29 of these devoted workers have either completed terms
of service, or for other reasons have decided to retire from the Inspectoral Corps .
This figure represents over 15 percent of the total number of Inspectors in the
Corps, and also includes 2 who have served a combined total of 82 years as
Inspectors.

1 Inspector has served 42 years-3 have served from 20 to 24 years- 7 have

from 5 to IO years and IOl, or 57% of the total lnspectoral Corps have served 5
years or less. 21 have served l year or less. The overall average length of service
for Inspectors is now 5.4 years, and this figure is dropping each year. We are
extremely grateful to each of the 29 Inspectors who have retired this year for their
loyalty and devoted service, but individual recognition should be given two of
our highly respected Senior Inspectors who have retired after serving notable

Lecturer was only 7 years old), Brother Niles Millar was appointed Inspector,

In 1938, Brother Guido DiGhetaldi was appointed Inspector, and he too,

significant program of activities to interest their Members; that most Lodges
were experiencing great difficulty in obtaining new Officer material; that 52 of
the 183 Inspectors reported that 208 of our Lodges were not filling the needs of
their Community, and that 62 Inspectors felt that in 248 of our Lodges, Masonry
was not advancing. In the following year, 1974, some slight changes for the good
were reported in all of these areas , but in their reports of July 1, 1976, the
Inspectors are reporting that 95 percent of all California Lodges are now carrying
on significant programs of activity; that only 46 percent of the Lodges are
reporting difficulty in obtaining new Officer material; That 98 percent of the
~odges are filling the needs of their community, and that Masonry is advancing
in 92 percent of all California Lodges! From this it is evident that the admonitions
of the past have been heeded, and that the Lodges have taken remedial steps to
reverse a negative trend in Masonry within this Grand Jurisdiction. These reports
also indicate that 95 percent of the Lodges have conducted satisfactory programs
of Ritual instruction, both at the District and the individual levels; also, that a
significant number of Lodges have participated in some Grand Lodge activity
during the year; and best of all . . . total Lodge donations to the Masonic Homes
Endowment fund have again this year exceeded the one million dollar mark!
From all this one might assume that there are no problems in California
Masonry. Unfortunately, this is not so. The same reports which indicate changes
for the good, also reflect some rather persistant problems to which our attention
should be directed.
It is a most distressing fact that a large majority of all Lodges in California are
still plagued by two major problems. Number one is declining membership and
number two is, disinterested membership. The first problem has several causative factors: deaths, <limits, suspension for nonpayment of dues and most
important-lack of Candidates for the degrees.
The second problem is one that is not uncommon to all other Fraternal and
Social organizations. Its cause seems to defy definition, but its effects are felt in
the Lodges in lack of attendance at degree meetings and social events, lack of
support for Lodge programs, and a general apathy among many of our members .
This problem can only be resolved by greater membership involvement, and
programs of high interest to the members. Sideliners nights and increased
membership participation in degree work can work miracles in increased interest
and attendance.
As to problem number one, aging membership and death of members is
something over which we have no control. Suspension for nonpayment of dues is
something which can, and should be controlled. It actually requires very little
effort to convince a Brother of the folly of forfeiting his Masonic membership by
not paying his dues, and a good active delinquent dues committee can work
wonders in cutting down these suspensions. Now, lets talk about the lack of
Candidates for the Degrees . This is a problem of our own making and one which
in my opinion, should not be permitted to continue! Masonry has far too long
hidden its attributes behind an almost in penetrable curtain of secrecy. This
curtain has been thoughtlessly woven by threads of misinformation and sheer
Masonic ignorance. If this curtain is ever to be parted, and thousands of new,
young and worthy applicants attracted to our Order, then we'd better start right

LEADERSHIP

In the Grand Lecturer's report last October, I announced that the Ritual
Committee had initiated a series of Leadership Seminars at the Division level. I
can now report to you that those seminars were a total success in every respect. It
seems that this approach to Masonic Education and leadership training fills a
need of the Lodge and the Brethren, for all who attended these sessions expressed
their desire that they be continued. After a great deal of study and discussion, the
Grand Master and the Elective Line Officers have determined that the leadership
program should be carried on by another Committee with the aid and support of
the Ritual Committee. The Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility has been chosen as the one to carry this program forward, and it has been
agreed that the all day Leadership Seminars shall be continued, but with some
modification. The Ritual Committee will conduct the first half of the Seminar,
and their efforts will be devoted strictly to instruction in the Ritual, Masonic Law
and Masonic Protocol. Following this, the committee on Masonic Information
and Responsibility will utilize the second half of the seminar for instruction in
Leadership and Masonic education.
. Judging from the results of previous Seminars, it is evident that the Brethren
will support such an educational program, and the craft will be greatly benefitted
by it. I urge all Brethren who have not attended these seminars to plan now to be
in attendance at the next one which occurs in your Division or area . You will be
well rewarded for your effort.
CONDITION OF THE LODGES

I have spent many hours in careful analysis of the Inspectors' Annual report
forms, for it is here, in the statistics, answers and opinions of the Inspectors that
the true condition of the Lodges is revealed.
It was pleasing to note this year that improvements have been made in most
Lodges in the areas of Lodge Activities, Officer procurement and community
involvement. As a comparison, in the Grand Lecturer's report of October, 1973 ,
it was reported that a great majority of the Lodges were not carrying on a

now to get off our duff and tell others what we all know about Masonry. .
That it is the finest Fraternal organization in the world, and that it builds
character in men through the teaching of great moral principals; and that here, in
Masonry, each man may seek the truth in his own way, completely unfettered by ·
all except that Universal Masonic belief in one Supreme being, whose miracles
are wrought through the Brotherhood of man . We don't need to ask men to join
Masonry-We need only tell them all about Masonry, and they'll ask us!
The Layman's Night in the Lodges has proven to be an excellent vehicle for
telling non-Masons all about Masonry. In the past year, it has been my pleasure
to be the speaker at seven of these Layman's Night programs in various Lodges
throughout the State, and I am quite pleased to report that as a direct result of
those informational meetings, thirty-five good men asked for petitions for the
degrees of Masonry in those seven Lodges. I most heartily recommend this
program to all Lodges, especially those who are not receiving petitions from
prospective candidates. All of us in the Ritual Committee have the necessary
information to plan and execute such a meeting. We will share it with anyone
who is interested .

and a heart full of love, given us by one who could very well write the book on
the three principal tenets of Masonry ... A past Master many times over-a 92
year young Mason-Worshipful James Clapper. "May God grant him many
additional years of life."
In our meeting with the Brethren of Kilauea Lodge in Hilo, we were pleased to
observe that many of the problems of the past have been resolved. This Lodge
presently has a full line of Officers, and activities within the Lodge and the
Community are on the increase. At the request of the Master, Worshipful Larry
Sumida, the Ritual Committee exemplified the Third degree for the Brethren,
and the discussion which followed removed several inconsistencies in the work.
It was good to meet with our old friends in Hilo, and to see Kilaeua Lodge
working in Peace and Harmony . In Maui, we were requested by the Master,
Worshipful William Foster, to conduct a mock Masonic Trial in the Lodge. The
Lodge Officers participated in this trial by acting as Trial Commissioners. They
heard the complete testimony and then rendered their verdict and affixed the
penalty. As a result of this demonstration it is felt that the Officers of Lodge Maui
now possess a much greater degree of understanding regarding Masonic Law and
Trial procedure. Masonry is extremely active in the Valley Isle, and new
Candidates are being received on a regular basis. Under its present leadership,
Lodge Maui has the capability of reasonable growth and great good within the
Community.
All of the Lodges on Oahu seem to be working in Peace and Harmony, and in
most, new Candidates are being received. Community activity continues to grow
in the Lodges there, and Ritual proficiency is at a most acceptable level in all the
Lodges in and around Honolulu.
The two Island Inspectors, Bill McKee and Ozzie Lau, continue to do their
usual fine job assisting all ten of the Hawaiian Lodges. These two dedicated
Masons are tirelds in their efforts to aid and assist the Officers and Brethren
within their Districts. They have clearly demonstrated their ability as expert
Ritualists and true Masonic leaders. We are extremely proud to have them in the
Inspectoral Corps, and we consider them to be our personal friends as well. To
all of our many good friends in Hawaii, Mahalo and Aloha. Aloha from the
bottom of our hearts.

HAWAIIAN MASONRY

Each time I visit Hawaii, I am overwhelmed at the warm hospitality of our
Hawaiian Brethren. They have the uncanny ability of making each visit seem a
little nicer than the one before .
This year, with the approval of Grand Master Roberts, the Ritual Committee
conducted a Masonic Leadership Seminar in the City of Honolulu. This all day
Seminar was held in the Scottish Rite Temple on Saturday, July 23rd, and in
addition to exemplification and instruction in the Ritual, it also covered such
subjects as Lodge Administration, Community involvement, a Mason's duty and
Masonic Trial procedure. There were present many Officers and members from
each of the seven Lodges on Oahu, and Officers or Representatives from each of
the three outer island Lodges. Judging from the enthusiasm of those who were
present, it is our feeling that a great deal of information and understanding was
imparted to the Brethren in this session. We were also delighted that the Grand
Master was present at this Seminar, and the message of encouragement which he
brought to the Brethren was most enthusiastically received. Following this
Seminar, special meetings and schools of instruction were held in each of the
outer island Lodges.
Kauai Lodge continues to experience severe difficulties in recruitment of
Officers and waning membership. Their problem lies in the fact that the total
membership of the Lodge is less than 100-only 19 live on the Island of Kauai.
There are also 13 Sojourners who live on the island, 2 or 3 of whom do attend the
meetings of Kauai Lodge. Despite these severe handicaps, there still exists
among the Brethren of Kauai, an indomitable spirit, and a firm resolve to rebuild
Kauai Lodge into a viable, active and useful part of Masonry in the Hawaiian
Islands. We commend them for their efforts. A high point of our trip to Kauai
was our visit to the home of James Clapper, Junior Past Master of Kauai Lodge.
The entire Ritual Committee joined with Brother Jimmie in a belated celebration
of his 92nd birthday, and we all came away with a greater appreciation for life,

CEREMONIES

At the suggestion of our good friend, Past Grand Master Chester R. MacPhee,
the Ritual Committee has undertaken a comprehensive study of the California
Masonic Funeral Service toward the possibility of modifying certain portions of
the language therein.
A complete revision and updating of the Handbook for Candidates' Coaches
was completed by the Ritual Committee this year, and the new copies of this
Handbook are both accurate and attractive. Revision of the Masters' Handbook
are also under way with a re-print of that manual not expected before the end of
next year.
It has been the feeling of the Ritual Committee for some time, that the present
Grand Lodge Ceremony for presentation of 50-year Veterans Buttons leaves a lot
to be desired. Some of its present wording is now totally inaccurate, and the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Ceremony on the whole, falls far short of conveying the warmth and appreciation
which we feel should be shown our 50-year Veterans. It is my recommendation
that the Grand Lodge Ceremony for presentation of 50-year Veterans Buttons be
completely rewritten to correct present inaccuracies in language, and to more
properly convey the true feelings of our Grand Lodge to recipients of the 50-year
Veterans Button.

1976-77 BUDGET
We are very proud of the fact that the Ritual Committee finished the 1975-76
Grand Lodge year several hundred dollars under the amount which was budgeted
for that period. This is due to restraint and good management on the part of the
Inspectors and the Assistant Grand Lecturers. Even though food and lodging
costs continqe to spiral upward, I feel that we can hold the line on expenses.
We have therefore requested a Ritual Budget in the amount of $49,500.00 for
the 1976-77 Grand Lodge year. This figure is only one percent higher than that
which was requested for last year.
CONCLUSION

If time permitted it would be my desire to individually express personal
gratitude to all who have assisted the Ritual Committee in their appointed tasks
this past year. There are so many.
The Masters of the Lodges, and their Officers who have made our job so much
easier by their cooperation and understanding- the various Grand Lodge Committeemen who have worked in our behalf-the 177 Masonic Inspectors who
have labored so diligently in teaching the Ritual amongst their many other
duties-the Six Assistant Grand Lecturers, without whose complete support this
Grand Lecturer could not function-the Grand Secretary and all the members of
his wonderful staff, without their assistance our job would have been extremely
difficult, if not totally impossible to perform-the wonderful gang of Grand
Lodge Officers for 1976 who have performed so well this year at all Grand Lodge
openings and Ceremonies, and last, but far from least, our Grand Master who has
given us all purpose and direction as he went about the business of promoting
Masonry in California this year. A man for whom I personally have the highest
regard, Most Worshipful John F. Roberts, Jr. Thank you Most Worshipful, and
thank you my Brethren, for your understanding and support, and for your
confidence in electing me to serve as your Grand Lecturer.

Respectfully submitted,
H. DOUGLAS LEMONS , Grand Lecturer

ANNUAL REPORT
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

What gifts you have given! Health, education, safety, comfort, companionship
and love all made possible by the Brethren through the exercise of your Masonic
belief IN RELIEF and Brotherly Love!
It is in this grateful tenor that the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of
California takes pride in delivering the Eighty-fourth Report of its policy, plans,
organization, administration and financial condition to this Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge covering the fiscal year July 1, 1975 through June 30, 1976.
ORGANIZATION OF THE BOARD:

The Masonic Homes of California is a charitable corporation organized and
existing pursuant to the laws of the State of California. The responsibility for the
operation of its benevolent purposes rests with a Board of Trustees which is
twelve in number, including the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior and Junior
Grand Wardens who serve as trustees by virtue of their respective offices. The
Grand Treasurer and the Grand Secretary are, respectively, the treasurer and
secretary of the Board. The other officers consisting of a president and one or
more vice-presidents are elected by the trustees at the organizational meeting
immediately following the close of the Grand Lodge Annual Communication
each year.
As of June 30, I 976 the Board was comprised of the following nine trustees
appointed by Grand Masters for terms which expire at the close of the Annual
Communication in the year indicated:

ORGANIZATION OF THE STAFF:

Our former Executive Director, Jack D. Billingsley, served admirably in an
extremely fast changing legislative atmosphere. Effective upon his resignation
for personal reasons, former Trustee Raymond A. Howe, the recently retired
Business Manager of the renowned and highly respected Palo Alto Medical
Clinic, was retained as his successor. Brother Howe not only brings to the Homes
his vast knowledge in the field of management; but his familiarity with our entire
operation, our Administrators and the Decoto rehabilitation program in particular, combines to make his selection a great addition to our management team.
During the year we also lost the valuable services of Decoto Administrator
Joseph M. Olafson who resigned his position for reasons of health. Because of
the depth built into our organization, Assistant Administrator J. Burton Brown,
who led our Skilled Nursing Facility operations, and who had the necessary
licensure and ability, was ready to move directly into the Administrator's
position. Michael Fitz, a graduate of the University of Arizona School of
Gerontology, has been employed to replace Brother Brown as Assistant Administrator.
James C. Blaine, the Administrator of our Homes for Children at Covina,
brought particular honor to California Masonry this year while serving as the
President of the Masonic Homes Executive Association of North America. This
important organization allows Trustees and Administrators of all North American
Masonic Homes to exchange information and to participate in educational
programs.
Brother Jim has added strength to the management of the Children's Home by
training Barry Antos to fill the office of Assistant Administrator.
Field Investigators Sue Collins (Northern California) and Martha Quick
(Southern California) continue their essential services in meeting the applicants,
their families, Lodge representatives and others; preparing written reports for the
Trustees; and generally easing the transition for our guests from their community
surroundings into our Homes. Professional guidance is also provided by these
competent and compassionate ladies for those in need of long term financial
assistance outside of our Homes, the program known as Outside Relief.
OPERATIONS:

The Trustees continue to meet monthly, alternately in the North and South to
conduct the general business of the Homes. Additionally, various committees of
the Board meet regularly at each of the Homes for the consideration of such
matters as scholarships, major maintenance and rehabilitation, and generally to

FINANCE:

We have been successful in renting a substantial portion of our unused land to
Glad A Way Gardens, a commercial flower firm. As a result we have substantially increased the rental income and made the area more attractive to our guests
and their visitors.
Just as in the management of our own homes and businesses, the operation of
the Masonic Homes continues each year to be more costly, notwithstanding
careful study and cost reduction programs. Not only has legislation required
additional payroll and construction expenditures, but the rehabilitation program,
as presently contemplated, will require an expenditure of twelve to fifteen
million dollars over the next three years.
The Masonic Homes Endowment Committee chaired by Worshipful Brother
Robert E. Hilts continues its outstanding work and has again exceeded one
million dollars in contributions through the Lodges this year. Requests by wills
continue on an upward trend as do living gifts of all types to the Masonic Homes.
The Pooled Income Fund and allied estate planning programs, which can save
large sums otherwise spent for taxes and administrative expenses by the estates of
the donors, maintain their successful course.
Notwithstanding these programs, the assignment of twelve to fifteen million
dollars from income producing assets to the rehabilitation program will correspondingly reduce our investment income. We must, therefore, redouble our
effots to replace those funds at the earliest possible date.
As in past years, the complete financial posture of the Masonic Homes and the
opinion of its auditors will be found in the published Proceedings of the Grand
Lodge.
SUMMARY:

Our California and Hawaii Masons truly have carried forth our charge to
"Care for our Own" and we can and should take great pleasure in that
accomplishment. Each member of the Board of Trustees of your Homes,
although required to devote innumerable hours of service each year, is truly
grateful to our Grand Master for affording us this opportunity.
Our respectful thanks we give to M.W. Chester R. MacPhee not only for
timely words of caution concerning the preservation of the funds of our Homes,

II. BUILDINGS
Refurbishing of all hallways, parlors, and public spaces has been completed.
This included painting, carpeting, and installation of drapes. The decor and
complimenting furnishings are different on each of the four floors throughout the
facility. In addition, all rooms in Wollenberg and Adams buildings were
repainted.
These beautiful improvements represent the collective thoughts and hours of
consideration that have been contributed by our Board of Trustees, the Rehabilitation Committee, and past and present administration.
Upgrading our kitchen equipment, improvement of food preparation, services,
and redecorating the temporary dining area has been approved by the Board of
Trustees and we look forward to this project being completed in the very near
future.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF ADMINISTRA TOR---COVINA HOME

Jackie Kulp, Glassell Park #605, was selected to continue her study of French
with a family in France. She will leave for six months in September, 1976.

It is a pleasure to submit the Annual Report of the Masonic Home for Children
for the year 1975-1976.
The following young men graduated this year from high school: Gary Meyers,
Sunnyside Lodge #577; Michael Welch, Signal Lodge #543, and Kevin Gould,
Lancaster Lodge #437. Residents re-united with their families this past year
were:

September 1st, a group of 26 residents and 4 staff members embarked on a
10-day Bicentennial tour of Philadelphia and Washington, D.C., thanks to the
Board of-Trustees and the Masonic Homes of New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
During the past year we have welcomed many new staff members including
Mr. Barry P. Antos, The Assistant Administrator and Director of Resident
Services, and Mr. Alfred Friend, the Activities Director! Both these men bring
added dimensions into the lives of the children in our care.
Among the various groups visiting the Masonic Home at Covina during
1975-76 were:

Merit School of Court Reporting

Masonic Home living continues to be exciting, meaningful and interesting!
Three Masonic Home Rainbow Girls were guests at the Hawaiian Grand
Assembly in Honolulu in June-thanks to the KeAnuennue Assembly at Kailua.
They were Laurie Torrace, (San Marino #685) Cindy Richardson (Fresno #247)
and Susan Pedretti (Illinois). We also had the pleasure of hosting a group of
Hawaii Rainbow Girls for Supreme Assembly in Anaheim in July.

30 Masonic Lodges
32 Job's Daughters Bethels
16 Rainbow Assemblies
13 "other" (Eastern Star, Golden Slipper, DeMolay, etc.)
Alumni Day was held this year on April 24th, with over 250 Alumni from the
United States in attendance for dinner and many happy hours of reminiscing.
Another reunion is planned for next year.
Health problems have been minimal this past year, thanks to preventive
medicine and education. Magan Medical Clinic continues to be our medical
resource, ably assisted by Ruby Thacker, our nurse.
A five-year preventive maintenance and equipment replacement program was
adopted by the Trustees. While costs of operation continue to escalate, an
on-going program is used to keep costs within bounds. Red Grande, Director of
Facility Services.is especially helpful.
We welcomed Brother Ray Howe as the new Executive Dir~ctor and sincerely
thank the Board of Trustees for their continuing help and especially thank the
Brothers of our great jurisdiction for their support.
Respectfully submitted,
JAMES C. BLAINE, Administrator

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

LODGES WITH LARGEST AVERAGE GIFTS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:

Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board submits its 44th Annual Report
covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1976. We again exceedeq the million
dollar mark for the 4th straight year.
INCOME FROM THE PERMANENT ENDOWMENT FuND
Income from the Permanent Endowment Fund amounted to $1,742,860.49,
which amount was transferred to the operating account of our two Homes. Each
year it becomes more evident of the wisdom of those early Masons who
established this Fund.

RECOGNITION TO LODGE SECRET ARIES
The Secretaries play a very important roll in the success of our program, and
we extend our sincere thanks to them.
RECOGNITION FOR SPECIAL GIFTS
Each year we have Brethren who help support our Homes with substantial gifts
to the Endowment Fund. To them we give our sincere thanks.
PRINTED MATERIALS FOR DISTRIBUTION
We encourage each Lodge to avail itself of the attractive and informative
literature on display in the exhibit area . We feel that distribution of these
pamphlets will encourage the support of our members .
SERVICE ROLL CERTIFICATES
Tabs for those Lodges who made the 1976 Service Roll have been sent to the
Lodges for placement on their certificates. Lodges who may be making the list
for the first time will receive a "Certificate" and a tab.
