CONCLUSION

Special thanks to our Grand Master, the Most Worshipful John F. Roberts, Jr.,
for his leadership and support in bringing the message to our members throughout the Jurisdiction.
We sincerely thank the Grand ·Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters, Grand
Lodge Committeemen and Inspectors for their support. To the Grand Lecturer,
Assistant Grand Lecturers, Masters, Wardens, and Lodge Endowment Committees, thanks again for contributi ng to make this another successful year.
We are most grateful to the 103,174 Brethren who contributed $1,037,406.84
to the Permanent Endowme nt Fund.
It is a most rewarding experience for the members of the Endowment Board to
have the opportunity of participating in this worthy program.

Board. One meeting was held during Grand Lodge Week and all member Lodges
and Officers of the Bureaus were invited to meet with the Board. The June 19,
1976 meeting was held to review and approve the proposed budgets for the 19
Bureaus for their operating income and expenses for the next Masonic year.
TAXES

All Bureaus prepared and filed the required information returns to the Internal
Revenue Service and the State Franchise Tax Board as well as the other required
quarterly and annual payroll tax forms.
T~e Board of Control expresses deep appreciation to W. Stanley Davis,
Chairman of the Taxation Committee, for his continued assistance on tax matters
as they apply to the Service Bureaus.

Referred to Committee on Finance (Budget allocation).

AUDITS

Audits of the administrative and financial activities of the following Bureaus
were made:

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Board of Control is pleased to submit its annual report for the 1975-76
Grand Lodge year. The members of the Board are deeply appreciative of the
opportunity to be associated with the Officers of the nineteen Masonic Service
Bureaus in this great Jurisdiction. These dedicated Officers of the Masonic
Service Bureaus give freely of their time and talents to direct the activities of the
Bureaus. These men also contribute to the tenets of Masonry by relieving the
distresses of Sojourners, the families, widows and orphans who reside in the area
served by the Bureau.
The Right Worshipful Kermit A. Jacobson, Deputy Grand Master, was
appointed Liason Officer to the Board of Control by the Grand Master, and he
has provided the Board with valuable counsel and assistance on many important
matters. His assistance and understanding were appreciated.
CORRESPONDENCE

A summary of all correspondence to and from the Board of Control and the
Service Bureaus and others was sent to the Deputy Grand Master and each
member of the Board of Control. The minutes of the Board of Control meetings
were sent to the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, the Grand Wardens,
Grand Secretary as well as the members of the Board.
MEETINGS

The Board held four meetings during the year. Two meetings were with the
Officers of the Bureaus, one was held in Northern California with 16 Officers in
attendance and one meeting in Southern California with 22 Officers in attendance. A two way communication was emphasized and the meetings proved
valuable both to the Officers of the Bureaus as well as to the members of the

San Gabriel
Pasadena

Long Beach
Los Angeles

East Bay
Southern Alameda
County

UNIFORM COMPACTS

Maya Lodge No. 793 relocated its meeting place, withdrew from the Los
Angeles Bureau and a new Uniform Compact with the San Gabriel Bureau was
approved.
Composite Lod~e No. 639 relocated its meeting place, withdrew from the Los
Angeles Bureau and a new Uniform Compact with the Santa Monica Bureau was
approved.
As the result of the consolidation of Lodges, a new Uniform Compact was
approved for Occidental-California Lodge No. l; Ingleside Pyramid Lodge No.
562; Brotherhood Lodge No. 375; George Washington Lodge No. 435; Educator
Lodge No. 554; Oriental Lodge No. 114 and Golden Gate Speranza Lodge No.
30 with the San Francisco Bureau. A new Uniform Compact was approved for
Henry Knox Westlake Lodge No. 392; Sunset Lodge No. 352 and Manhattan
Lodge No. 742 with the Los Angeles Bureau. A new Uniform Compact was
approved for Culver City Lodge No. 476 and Westchester-Madison Lodge No.
572 with the Santa Monica Bay Bureau.
ANNUAL REPORTS

. All .Bureaus have supplied the annual reports, election, budget, statistical and
fmancial returns. (see appendices)
NEW SECRET ARIES

Emanuel Beber retired as Secretary of the Richmond Bureau and was replaced
by Fred R. De Barrows. Lee 0. Shrock retired as Secretary of the Los Angeles

Bureau and was replaced by William R. Helms, and Dudley D. Manlove was
appointed Assistant Secretary. Ralph W. Thorell retired as Secretary of the
Pasadena Bureau and was replaced by Lewis P. Reiterman.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DISTRIBUTION

130

BUSH MASONIC RELIEF

Sincere apprec1at1on is expressed to Ralph H. Head, President, and the
Directors of the Bush Masonic Relief Corporation. This Corporation provides
much needed funds for the operation of the six Masonic Service Bureaus located
in the Greater Los · Angeles Area. Their contribution amounted to over
$56,000.00 or 53% of the total budget of $105,900.00 for all Bureaus in this
Grand Jurisdiction for the Masonic year 1976-77. The contribution is material
and means a great deal to the member Lodges who are the recipients.
INSURANCE

All Bureaus were informed by a general letter prepared by Thompkins and
Company, the insurance carrier for Grand Lodge. It clarified the insurance
coverage relative to the Service Bureaus.
APPRECIATION

The Board expresses deep appreciation to each of the Executive Secretaries,
the Officers and the many committee men of all Bureaus for their dedicated
devotion to the welfare of the Sojourning Masons. Special appreciation is
extended to the Grand Master, the Grand Lodge Officers and particularly to the
Grand Secretary and his very capable staff.
The Board of Control functioned within its Budget this year and herewith
requests the sum of $1,300.00 to cover anticipated expenses during the ensuing
year.

I3I

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
After reviewing the Grand Master's Annual Message, the Reports of the Grand
Treasurer, Grand Secretary, Masonic Homes Trustees and the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board, the Committee on Distribution submits the following report:
GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

The Grand Master's Message contains one decision and five recommendations. We recommend that the subject matter involved in the Grand Master's
Message be referred to Committees as follows:
Decision with regard to the expenditure of five thousand dollars ($5,000), to
provide for the rebuilding of Quitman Lodge No. 88 Temple, be referred to the
Committees on Finance and Temple Properties.
Recommendation number one with regard to the dollar amount for the term
"nominal" in Section 410f and g (Old Code) and Section 2318 (New Code), be
referred to committees on Policy and General Purposes and Code Commission.
Recommendation number two with regard to a pilot travel tour sponsored by
the Grand Lodge of California be referred to the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes.
Recommendation number three with regard to a Grand Master's decision being
valid only for his year, unless a resolution is presented in the usual manner at a
subsequent Annual Communication be referred to the committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and "General Purposes.
Recommendation number four with regard to an applicant being obligated on
other than the Holy Bible be referred to the committees on Ritual and Jurisprudence.
Recommendation number five with regard to eligibility for fifty year pins be
referred to the Committees on Ritual and on Policy and General Purposes.

Respectfully submitted,
WARREN W. WILDMAN, Chairman
D. EWING MARSH
JOSEPH L. OUSLEY
FRANK D. ROSEN
ARTHUR R. KIRK

At the close of the 1975 Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, the
Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its Annual
Meeting. The Board of Trustees then proceeded to nominate and elect the
following officers to serve for the ensuing year until new ones are elected:
DeWald M. Baum .. .... .................... . .. .President

Edward H. Siems, P.G.M ....... ... ..... .. ... . .. .Secretary

This year our Masonic Temple celebrated its eighteenth birthday. Because new
Officers of the Constituent Lodges, together with many of the Brethren attend
Grand Lodge for the first time, your Trustees believe that it is appropriate to
remind them that our magnificent building was conceived and built by California
Masons as their permanent headquarters. It was a dream of dedicated and
far-seeing men that required eleven years of great vision and frustration before its
final satisfactory construction. It can be truly said that when our Brethren
determined to build a Grand Lodge Headquarters of their own, they let no
obstacles interfere with their magnificent dream. Masons have from time
immemorial been called builders of beautiful edifices . This building is concrete
evidence that we truly practice the fine principles that we teach.
Our California Masonic Memorial Temple, located at the top of prestigious
Nob Hill, has each year successively added to its glowing reputation as an
outstanding complex for the cultural, civic and educational activities of San
Francisco. The building represents our very substantial contribution to the
beautification of this great metropolitan city and the promotion of the fine arts
and sciences. We fervently hope and pray that the Great Architect of the
Universe will continue to permit this structure to shine as a beacon light of our
Fraternity's determination to support and advance a free public school system for
the education of the many generations of Americans yet to be and that it signify
to all who view it tangible evidence of our determination to make the world a
better place for all people in which to live .
Our 3165 seat auditorium accoustically is excellent for concerts, lectures and
the performance of musical and dramatic presentations. Business organizations,
fraternal societies, state governmental departments and professional associations
are continually increasing their use of our facilities for their meetings and trade
shows. It has proven by experience and use that it is an excellent showcase for all
their diverse, demanding and numerous activities.

The Temple is open daily, except Saturday and Sunday, for our many visitors
from 9:00 A.M. to 4:30 P.M. If there are other activities in the Temple on

PUBLICA TION BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F . & A. M . of California:
The Grand Master. the Grand Secretary. such advisors as deemed desirable.
and an Editor-In-Ch ief appointed by the Grand Master constitute the Publication
Board of Grand Lodge and as such respon sible for the publish in g and distribution
of the California Freemason.
The magaz ine has no w completed its 23rd year of publication and during thi s
period has issued nearly 14.000,000 copies . During the past year 884.000 iss ue~
were mailed to members of California Lodges. to paid subscribers. and to
jurisdictions both in the United States and in forei gn countries.
The California Free mason has but one mission: to bring the good news about
Free masonry to the Masons of California. to the O fficers of the subordinate
Lodges, to those who regularly atte nd Lodge meetings. and, just as important. to
those who, for many reasons do not or can not partic ipate as active ly as in the
past.
During the past year mo re than 175 Lod ge. Di strict. and Grand Lodge event~
were reported both pictorially and verbally in the four quarte rly issues. Article~
on Masonic Homes, scholarships granted by the California Masonic Fo undati on.
student essays generated by Public Schools Week and Constitut ion Month
o bservances have all found their way into print. The Bicente nnial Year has been
celebrated with 25 artic les and stories on the part Freemusonry has played in the
founding and growth of o ur country .
All of the reportorial accomplishm ents enumerated are only as worthwhile a~
the readers of the magazine decide them to be. and nothing would make the
Editor happier than to be required to print two -even three and four page~ of
.. letter~ to the editor" in which California Mason ~ express their opinions-no t
only about the virtues and the shortcomings of the magazine- but abo ut what
might best be tenned "for the good of the Order." Don't let a 13 cent stamp
stand in the way of making your voice heard. fo r only in this way will the
California Free ma son best serve Masonry in California and Hawaii .
Fo r several years the per capita cost of the magaz ine has been 40 cents pe r
annum . Paper and production costs-not editorial - have increased finally to the
extent that with regret the Publication Board requests an increase of 10 ce nt s to a
total of 50 cents a year or 12 1/2 cents a copy. Even at that price , we still ho pe you
belie ve it will be a good buy.

Res pec tfully submitted.

FOR FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE 30. 1976

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
It is with pleasure that the In vestme nt Committee reports a s uccessfu l fiscal
year which ended on June 30, 1976.
The first quaner of 1976 saw the stock market move from a low below 800 on
the Dow Jones Industrial Average to a high of over IOOO in Ma,rc h . At the same
time, in April of 1976. y ields on high grade long-tenn bond~ reached the lowest
levels since the cyclical peaks reached in the fall o f 1974 . Both of these factors
resulted in market value improveme nt in the Grand Lodge investment ponfolio
under superv ision of your Investment Com mittee . The portfolio increased in
value from $48,430,885 on June 30, 1975 to $57, 731,221 on June 30, 1976 .
Income earned from the ponfolio increased from $2.737,351 to $3,335 ,882
annually or a gain of 21 % . It is interesting to note that more than 50% of t he
common stock issues held in the portfolio inc reased their dividend during the
fiscal year.
Government and high-grade corporate bonds repre sent 37% of the market
value of the portfolio, with an average weighted maturity of 16 years and an
average weighted coupon of 7.32c.K. Quality-wise all of the issues held are rated
investment grade by the in vestment rating services and the avemge weighted
quality is c lose to Aa.
The convertible bonds and preferred s tocks make up 13% of the portfolio's
market value . These issues arc currently returning 6.3% at market and with the
increase in value of stock prices the market value of the conve rt ible portion of the
portfolio has moved up with the stock prices.
Common stocks· continue to represent approx imately 50% of the fund. O ver
the past year. the market value increased 8.4% without consideration for the
dividend income which currently is 4% based on the market value. This increase
take s into account adju~tments for gifts and bequests made in kind duri ng the
year.
Our investment adviser , Alliance Capital Management Corporation, during the
year conti nued to recommend securities that meet our investment objectives
which we recognize to be maximum income commensurate with the safety of
principal. As fiduciaries we are guided by the California statute which is
commonly known as the .. prudent man" investment rule . Our investment
strategy is to maintain a proper halance between fixed income securities and
equities, to buy and hold quality i s~ues only, and to maintain recommended
industry weightings within the stock portion of the portfolio.
The economic recovery has progressed much as forecast by Alliance Capital
which was expectation of a moderate, balanced ex pansion. There also seems to
be growing confidence in the belief that we will no t ~ee a return to double-digit
inflation, panicularly when one hxiks at the cautious pos ture of businessmen and
the recent favorable wage experiences in world economies. There is, admittedly ,
some concern that selected industries will face capacity tightness next year. but
generally there appears to be suffic ient manufacturing capacity to allow fo r a

146

moderate expansion through 1977. T his latter point seems to be supported by the
fact that the upsurge in plant and equipment expend itures has been de layed so far
in thi s cycle. It is Alliance·s belief that we are in the early to mid-stages of an
economic recovery. Federal Reserve Board actions. geared to a slowing of
expansionist tendencies, seem to be working based on the latest money supply
figures and the economy from here should experie nce a slower and more

It has been the policy of your Committee to consider the safety and preservation of capital as its primary goal. Nevertheless, recognition has been given to the

REPORT OF TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F . & A . M . of California:
Each year your Taxation Committee throug h you. cautions the various
organizations comprising Grand Lod ge as to the importance of the reports
required by the Federal Government and the State of California. Compliance
with the various tax laws is the responsibility of the elected and appointed
Officers and Trustees of all Masonic groups.
Under tax laws our organizations generally have been favored by tax exem ption. To maintain our tax exempt status certain re ports are required. It is esse ntial
these reports be filed timely. All tax-exempt organizations are coming under
muc h closer scrutiny by the Federal and State regul atory agencies. Lack of
compliance with the law will subject us to penalties and it wi ll be increasingly
difficult to maintain exempt status.
A ll Lodges having annual gross receipts in excess of $5 .000 mu st file I.R.S.
Form 990 "Return of Organization Exempt from Income Tax. " If a Lod ge fails
to file the return before the due date it will have to pay$ I 0 for eac h day the return
is late-not to exceed $5.000.
All Lodges must file California Franchise Tax Board Form 199 or 199 B
.. Exempt Organization Annual Information Return ." In case of failure to file on
time the Lodge will have to pay $5 for each month after the due date- not to
exceed $40.
Under the laws the penalties may be avoided if "it can be shown that the
failu re was due to reasonable cause ." Both the Internal Revenue Service and the

147

California Franchise Tax Board have made it known that " reasonable cause"
must be someth ing extraord inary and that penalties generally wi ll be assessed.
The ultimate penalty may also be applied resulting in the loss of tax exempt
status .
Wages paid to a Lodge employee may be subject to Federa l withholding tax
and social security taxes. Failure to file Form 941 .. Employer's Qu arterl y
Federal Tax Return" results in a penalty of 5% a month not to exceed a total of
25'k of the unpaid amount and interest of 7% a year.
Wages paid to a Lodge employee may be subject to California income tax
withholding. state disability insurance, and California unemployment insurance .
Failure to file Fonn DE 3 ·'Quarterly Contri buti on Re turn and Report of Wages
Under the Unemployment Insurance Code and Report of California Personal
Income Tax Withheld" will result in a penalty of 10% of the unpaid amount and
inte re st of V2% a month .
Service Bureaus must file these returns with the Internal Revenue Service and
the Franchise Tax Board .
Temple Associations must also file similar returns with the Internal Re ven ue
Service and the Franchise Tax Board. The return s used are determined by the
type of ownership of the Temple. In some instances the Temple is owned by the
Lodge, in wh ic h case the information required is included in the Lodge Form 990
and Form 199 or 199 B. In some instances the Temple is owned by a tax exempt
organization, in which case a separate Form 990 and Forn1 199 or 199 B is
required. In some cases the Temple is owned by a regular co rporation in wh ich
case the report wi ll be made on Form 1120 "U. S. Corporate Income Tax
Return" and California Fonn 100 "Corporate F ranchise Tax Return."
The problems reported by both the Federal and State autho ritie s include:
l.

2.

3.

Returns rec,eived after filing date and , in the case of California, without
filing fees.
Return s received wit hout the preprinted name a nd address label s supplied
by the government . These labels are coded with specific infom1ation and
assist in posting returns and fees to accounts.
Failure to reply to correspondence. This freq uently may be due to changes
of addresses and failure to forward mail.

The various entities of Grand Lodge have their own tax requirements, and we
urge the Officers and Trustees in the ir positions of responsibility to be thoroughly
infonned on the tax problems of the ir organizations.
In conclusion. your Committee reminds you a ll again that tax exempti on under
the law is a privilege. To maintain that privi lege, we must comply with the law .

AFTERNOON SESSION-T uesday, October 12, 1976

America in the 1976 Repon reaffirms its suggestion th at recognition of the Grand
Orient and of those State Grand Lodges that qualify would see m to be in order.
To me, the crux of the problem is that the only exceptions Gra nd Lodge has made
to the American doctrine of exclusive territorial jurisdiction has been in those
countries where the seve ral Grand Bodies are in amity and recognize each other
as legitimate. The doctrine referred to above was last enunciated by Grand Lodge
in the 1953 Proceedings. page 216, in the following words: "Territorial
Sovere ignty: It (the Grand Lodge) is an independent. self governing organization
having exclusive dogmatic Masonic authority over resident Masons and the three
symbolic degrees ." Actually. this is a st ricter test than the one found in the 1948
Proceedings, page 250. which require s independence. supreme authority over the
symbolic degrees , " and undisputed control over its constituent lodges. The
standard set forth by the Commission differs in that it would permit recognition
of a Grand Lodge which "shares such exclusive territorial jurisdiction wi th
another Grand Lodge by mutual consent or treaty." (Grand Lodge Recognition,
1956 ed. p . 69).
We believe that before we can ask Grand Lodge to modify our present law . so
as to recognize the Grand Orient, we should determine what relationship actuall y
exists between the State Grand Lodges and the Grand Orient and its State Grand
Orients. To thi s end our Grand Secretary has written to the eighteen Grand
Lodges we recognize in Brazil requesting informatio n on this matter.
Your Committee , therefore, repeats the recommendation embodied in its 1975
Report , that the Grand Lodge of California sho uld re serve consideration of this
matter until we have substantial evidence that a state of amity and mutual
recognition does actually exi st between the State Grand Lodges and the Grand
Orient.

Cuba
To conclude on an encouraging note , the problems presented by the influx of
refugee Cuban Masons are being solved. A small splinter group still claims to be
the Grand Lodge of Cuba in Exile and unfortunately has some success in
affiliating newly arrived Masons. False c laims arc made that the Grand Lodge in
Ex ile is recognized by several East Coast Jurisdictions. including New York. but
we learn that the New York Grand Body in que stion is known as La Serenissima
Gran Logia de Lcngua Espanola and is unknown to ei ther the Grand Lodge of
New York or the Grand Lodge of Cuba .
However. most of the Cuban Mason!. who have come to o ur shores. have
heeded Grand Master Tarajano's wise advice and have affiliated with the regular
Lodges near their place of residence . They have fonned a nationwide o rganization
called the Federacion de Masones Cubanos Desterrados. The Associations which
make up this Federati on permit no Masonic ceremonies. and of course do not
confer degrees . but they do provide a congenial place where Cuban Masons.
some of whom do not choose to join a regular Lodge. because of age. finances.
lack of Engli sh . or other reasons. can meet on a fraternal basis. The Associations
make a point of urging those Masons who can qualify to affi liate with American
lodges. and are ready with advice and help . There are four such associations in
California: the one in Orange County and the South Bay area named lndependencia is proud of the fact that over twenty-five DeMolays have fathers or
grandfathers in its membership. It was also a moving force in the erection and
donation to the City of Los Angeles of a stat ue of the great Cuban Patriot and
Ma~on Jose Mani on the a nni versary of his birthday. January 28. which is
cckbratcd in Cu ba as " Mason 's Day." Grand Lodge participated in the
dedication ceremo nies. the Deputy Grand Master o fficiating . Hi s dedication
address wa~ tra n ~ l atcd into Spanish by Bro. Aureliano Corcuba. who, with
Brothers Leandro Franco and Saulo Salvador ha ve been of significant importance
in effecting the harmonious adj ustment of our Cuhan Brothers to Freemasonry in
California.
The Grand Lodge of Cuba. in spite of governmental harassment. continues
working in its regular fonn.
It publishes a. mo nthly bulletin whic h is received by it~ memhcrs in this
country. its Grand Fucntionarics travel freely and constantly. Masons wea r

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
The primary responsibility of the Code Commission is to prepare the pocket
supplement to the California Masonic Code each year. This work is done during
and shortly after the Annual Comm unication. Following the 1975 Annual
Communication , your Commission incorporated the various amendments. additions and deletions to the Con titution a nd Regulatio ns into the new Masonic
Code al. well as selected and prepared annotatio ns from the Grand Master' s
Decisions. the G rievance Committee Report and the repo rts of other Grand
Lodge Boards and Committees. The Code Commissio n will work at the 1976
Annual Communicati9n to prepare the first supplement to the new Masonic
Code.
It is anticipated that the ne w revision of the Ca lifornia Masonic Code will
necessitate one or two meetings of the Code Commission in order to resolve the
minor proble ms that inevitably ari se with a new revision. We would therefore
request that our budget be inc reased to $1650.00 to cover any necessary
expenses.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAN D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In addition to the above listed Lodges , which have reported in regard to their
Bicentennial Celebration programs. the Committee is of the opinion that man y
other California and Hawaii Masonic Lodges, as well as many other Concordant Bodies. have likewise held successful Bicentennial Celebration programs in
1976; but that through inadvertence did not report the same to the Grand Lodge
Bicentennial Committee prior to the time the Committee's report was prepared in
September of this year.
From a review of the Bicentennial reports which have been forwarded to it, the
Committee is pleased 10 state that throughout our Grand Jurisdiction the Masters
of Masonic Lodges have appreciated the great opportunity they have had this
year to celebrate and recognize the importance of the sigining of the Declaration
of Independence two hunc..lred years ago, and to point out to their Brethren that
many of our predecessor Masonic Brothers were largely re'sponsible for this great
instrument. The language in this document , as well as that which later appeared
in the Constitution of the United States, is a masterpiece of clear thinking.
beautiful prose, and lofty ideals. We can well be proud of the fact that Masons
were so prominent in the meetings which led to rhe drafting of these two very
important documents.
[n additio n to the Masters wearing the three cornered colonial hat during Stated
Meetings thi s year and arranging at a Stated or other Meeting to call attention to
the Bicentennial subject, many Masonic Lodges participated in very large and
extensive Bicentennial programs, either through their own activity or in conjunctio n with other Lodges in their District. Sometimes the Masonic Lodges of a
number of Districts worked together upon a Bicentennial Celebration program .
Many of the Lodges in large Metropolitan areas cooperated well together and
sponsored a large city-wide or area-wide program . This was done in San
Francisco. Alameda, Long Beach, Los Angeles, San Diego, Fresno, and the
Lodges of Contra Costa County , as well as elsewhere in the State. All programs
were excellent and those participating therein deserve much credit.
The size of the Lodge did not necessarily indicate the type of program
undertake n or the result obtained. Little Georgetown Lodge No. 25, which is
located in the Motherlode lower mountain co untry between Placerville and
Auburn in Northern California, which has a membership of only eighty-one,
conducted an outstanding program which depicted the signing of the Declaration
of Independence two hundred years ago. This was a great accomplishment for so
small a Lodge in such a sparsely populated area .
Another relatively small Lodge, Nevada No . 13, with a membership of 242
located in Nevada City, again staged its outstanding Constitution Observance and
Bicentennial program on September 19th of this year with a parade which would
have done credit to any large metropolitan area . The parade lasted several hours
and was participated in by variou s units from all over Northern California and
Nevada. This Bicentennial Celebration program in NevaJa City was so outstanding that it was designated as an official California Bicentennial Project by the
State of California Bicentennial Commission .
There were several other truly very outstanding Bicente nnial programs around
our State. One of these was the February 16 , 1976 program of the San Francisco
Masters and Wardens Association , which celebration was held in the California

Grand Lodge Memorial Masonic Temple on the top of Nob Hill in San Francisco
where Brother Burl Ives was the outstanding character and entertainer in the
program. Another very outstanding Bicentennial program was that which was
sponsored by the Grand Lodge of California anJ the Long Beach Masters and
Wardens Association in the Long Beach Municipal Auditorium on May 22,
1976. This very entertaining and fast moving program was preceded by an
outstanding lengthy parade through downtown Long Beach , and all associated
with this entire program deserve much credit, for it was truly excellent in every
sense of that word. This Grand Lodge Long Beach Bicentennial program on May
22nd was designated as an official California Bicentinnial Celebration Project by
the State of California Bicentennial Commission.
Probably the most outstanding Bicentennial program of all was the one
sponsored by the California Grand Lodge in conjunction with the various
Masonic Lodges in Los Angeles and adjacent areas on Saturday, July 3, 1976.
Like the Lo ng Beach program. this was a mu sical episode depicting the two
hundred year history of the United States in music and song. [t w as a very
enjoyable, exciting two hour program.
Both the Los Angeles and the Long Beac h music programs were written by
Junior Grand Warden. Right Worshipful Donald G . Ingalls , with the very able
assistance of the Grand Lecturer , Very Worshipful H. Douglas Lemons, and Past
Master Jerry Rosen of Silver Trowel Lodge No. 415, who coordinated the
orchestrations for these two events . Both of these musical programs were very
enjoyable and well received by the many Masons and friend s who attend ed the se
events. with both auditoriums nearly filled to capacity.
The Los Angeles program was entitled "Music America," and in addition to
those mentioned above the following . also . lent their talents and were responsible
for much of the success of the program: Worshipful Ernest Hughes, the present
Master of Silver 'trowel Lodge No. 415 of Hollywood; Philip Gray. the present
Senior Warden of that Lodge; Marvin Miller, Paul H . Haines, Jr ., James
Doherty, Nick Lucas. Harvey Hunter, and Royal Dano , whose portrayal of
Abraham Lincoln giving the Gettysburg address was outstanding .
The program for this great Los Angeles celebration was as follows :

ABOUT SECRECY ..
It is true that we have modes of recognition, rites, and ceremonies , with which
the world is not acquainted. However. we are not a secret order. All true Masons
know that their work is not secret, but they realize that it must remain unknown
to all who do not live the Masonic life. If the so-called 1.ecrets of Freemasonry
were shouted from the housetops, the Fraternity would be absolutely safe. for
certain spiritual qualities arc necessary· before the REAL Masonic secrets can be
understood even by the Brethren themselve~. Hence it is. that the alleged
"exposures" of Freemasonry printed by the thousand~ and tens of thousands
since 1730 dmvn to the present hour. cannot injure the Fraternity. They reveal
merely the outward fom1s and ceremonies of Freemasonry. Only those who have
been weighed in the balance and found to be true, upright and square. have
prepared themselves by the ir own growth to appreciate the inner meaning of our
Craft. To the rest of the world. within or without the Lodge, our sacred rituals
must remain , as Shakespeare might have said, "'Words, words, words." Within
the Mason's own being is concealed the Power which constitutes the Builder' s
Word. His life is the sole password which admit s him to the true Masonic Lodge.

I LEAVE YOU THESE THOUGHTS TO PONDER UPON ...
As Masonic leaders of today. in meeting the challenge we face. we must have
a set of clearly defi ned goals and arrange a program that will be effective in
meeting the needs of the members. Our duty is clear. If Masonry is to prosper
during the next century. we must convince the world by our actions that we ARE
better men; that we ARE actively engaged in the industry of spreading useful
knowledge. practicing charity and inculcating goodwill among men. It is to the
everlasting credit of Freemasons that we have taken these great principles. t he
Brotherhood of Man and the Fatherhood of God, as our foundation and put them
into practice in daily life . To be a Mason is to be a friend to any man in need.
regardless of his race or creed.
America today desperately needs a great cause! She needs a noble and just
purpose. She needs tu catch the vision of a goal which calls for and is worthy of
.~acrifice and hard work.
Brethren. I suggest to you. WE are, indeed. the vehicle which can aid in
America' s searc h-that is. to ~timulate a re-dedication of duty to God. to our
Country, and to our fellow man through those basic principles ofour Fraternity !

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grund Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Publ ic Schools has endeavored during thi s past Gra nd
Lodge Masonic Year to carry forward the ideas and programs of fonner
committees and to initiate some innovati ons for imp lementation th is year and in
the fu ture. The hard working Committee consisted of twenty-nine members and
one consultant.
We have had the enthusiastic support and encouragement of our Grand Master,
Most Worshipful John F. Roberts. Jr., and the other Grand Lodge Elective Line
Office rs. as well N> the Grand Secretary and his staff. To all of them we ex.press
our profound thanks. particularly to Marian Thomas and her Supply Room staff.
The Grand Master and yo ur Committee Chainnan spent considerable effort to
all ocate the Committee members geographicly throughout our Jurisdiction and to
select 6 Division Coordinato rs to work with the Committeeme n in the six.
Di vis ions to assure that every Lodge be personally contacted by the Public
Schools Commiteee and assistance offered for a successful April 1976 Public
Schools Observance based on the theme PUBLIC SCHOOLS-OUR FUT URE .
The Grand Master proclaimed April as Publ ic Schools Month and encouraged
Masonic Lodges to be in contact with their local school departments to designate
a week during April as Publ ic Schools Week in their loca lity. The cooperation of
public officials and school administrators throughout California and Hawaii
re su lted in numerous supporting proclamations and p ronouncements reaching far
and wide to the general public.
The Grand Master appointed Right Worshipful Donald G. Ingalls as the laison
officer to our Committee. His assistance , knowled ge and cooperation were
abundant and greatly appreciated by this Committee.
Three full committee meetings were held durin g the yea r. The firs t was at the
Airport Marina Hotel in Los Angeles Saturday November 8. 1975. The second
was June 6, 1976 at the Americana Hotel near the Los Angeles Airport. T he final
one was held on Tuesday Morning during Grand Lodge week in Octobe r 19 76. In

the Hyatt Airport Hotel in Los Angeles on January 25, 1976 to finalize plans for

GENERAL PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY

Your Committee printed 20,000 posters, 40,000 table tents, 200,000 pamphlets and several thousand appreciation certificates. In January 1976 5 posters,
l 0 table tents, IO pamphlets and one appreciation certificate were mailed to each
incoming Master along with an order form for the Lodge to order more of these
materials. An order form was also sent to the Lodge Secretary under separate
cover. The response from the Lodges was most gratifying with most of the
materials being ordered and shipped out to the Lodges. We did not charge for the
pamphlets, but sent the quantity requested by the Lodge or enclosed 500 if no
larger amount was specificly requested.
In December your Committee mailed four articles regarding Public Schools to
the Lodges with the suggestion that the Masters use them in their January,
February, March and April Lodge Bulletins. In April, we mailed another article
for inclusion in the May Lodge Bulletin urging the Brethren to continue to
support and concern of our Public Schools throughout the year and not just in
April. Your Committee feels that our concern for our Public School System
should be a year-round project for our Grand Lodge and constituent Lodges.
Public Schools observance copy was mailed to the almost 500 radio stations in
California and Hawaii with a cover letter from the Grand Master. It was hoped
that the radio stations would read the copy during April as spot announcements.
Also two slides and copy were mailed to the almost 100 television stations in our
Jurisdiction for airing and viewing during April. In general, the cooperation was
abundant in the more rural areas and limited in the metropolitan areas. It is
recommended that a more personal contact be made with the radio and television
stations by the Brethren throughout California and Hawaii as the 1977 Public
.
Schools Observance approaches.
Many essay contests were held throughout our Jurisdiction, and the BiCENTENNIAL theme was abundantly employed in conjunction with Public
Schools Week Observances. Reports were sent to the Masters to complete and
return regarding their Lodge's activities. Almost 600 reports were received by
your Committee and have been analyzed with the hope of making future years'
observances more effective. Of particular note was the wide acceptance by the
Masters of the several Lodge Bulletin articles about Public Schools that were
used by the Masters.
In some areas Public Schools slogans were flashed on message boards, such as
at the San Francisco Giants and Los Angeles Dodgers baseball games and at
Golden Gate Fields where the message board is generally read by passing
motorists on U.S. highway 80. Also, the Bay Area Rapid Transit flashed Public
Schools slogans on their station message boards almost 2,000,000 times during
the month of April.
Many other local observance features were employed by Lodges and Districts
throughout our Jurisdiction and were reported to the Committee by the Masters'

reports. Many outstanding types of observances were held but are too numerous

GENERAL COMMENTS

On December 17, 1975 the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand
Secretary and your Committee Chairman journeyed to Sacra?1ento and spent t~e
latter part of the afternoon with Dr. Wilson Riles, Supenntenden~ of Pubhc
Instruction for the State of California. This meeting was most productive, and the
spirit of cooperation was abundant in the mutual effort to accomplish bett~r
things in our public educational system. Dr. Riles is~ue.d a lette.r dated m
February 1976 which was sent by him to all School Distnct Supenntendent~.
This Committee made copies for all Masters and mailed them to each Lodge. It is

be continued.
Concern was expressed during this past year that we as Masons and also. as
individuals do not and cannot condone many of the things that are presently being
done in our local schools, and that we must be careful not to let the general public
be of the opinion that we support all the actions and pro~s of ~ur many school
districts. What we do support is the concept of Pubhc Education and not the
specific programs of a particular school district. This point was discus~d at
length at our June 6, 1976 full Committee meeting and ~he afo~menttoned
conclusion was unanimously reached. The 1977 posters will say SUPPORT
PUBLIC EDUCATION" to help bring this important point into focus.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TEMPLE PROPERTIES

The Committee expresses its appreciation to Grand Master John F. Roberts,
Jr., for his assistance and total support; to Deputy Grand Master Kermit A.
Jacobson, who has served in a liaison capacity between the Committee and the
Grand Lodge Line Officers; and to the Grand Secretary and Assistant Grand
Secretary and their cooperative and efficient staff for their complete cooperation
and assistance throughout the year. Your Chairman has had throughout the year
the continuing support and cooperation of eight Committee members whose
knowledge and dedication have made possible our accomplishments.
In view of the continuing need for stationery, postage, and travel expense
necessary to the Committee functions, a request is made for a budget allocation
of $2,602.00 for 1976-1977 Masonic Year.

I76

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

The Committee on Temple Properties is pleased to submit its report of
activities during the past Masonic Year. The content of this report reflects that
inflation coupled with high interest rates has resulted in fewer Lodges and
Temple Associations proceeding with plans for the construction of new Temples
and an increase in the number electing to refurbish, repair and remodel existing
Temples. In consideration of the ever-increasing cost of maintenance, alterations, and construction, the Committee has submitted for your consideration at
this Annual Communication a resolution to increase from $2,500.00 to
$5,000.00 the amount a Lodge or Temple Association may spend for Temple
alterations without obtaining Committee approval.
It is encouraging to observe the foresight, dedication, and efforts displayed by
the Brethren of California and Hawaii in their continuing efforts to provide and
maintain suitable meeting places for our Masonic Family. They have continued
to demonstrate that Masonic Temples can be provided at equitable rental rates by
careful planning, and the utilization of the many skills of their members. Their
working together for a common goal is truly the spirit of Masonry.
The Committee is aware of the increasing concern of our Masonic Family for
the welfare and safety of those attending meetings at our Temples. We commend
those Lodges and Temple Associations that have taken positive action to provide
a safe meeting place by providing well-lighted and enclosed parking facilities,
security patrols, and escorting their guests to their cars at the conclusion of their
meetings.
There are within this Jurisdiction many Temples which are owned directly by
Lodges, some are owned by stock corporations, a few are owned by term
corporations, and others are owned by non-profit Corporations. Your Committee
strongly recommends the incorporation of Masonic Temple Associations under
the Non-Profit Law of the State of California to hold title and operate temple
properties. This type of corporation conforms to Masonic Law as well as the Law
of this State. The non-profit Corporation provides a means for raising funds
through the sale of contributing memberships, insulates the Lodge membership
from liability, provides continuity of management, ease in record keeping, and
conformity to tax laws. Your Committee is engaged in identifying the Lodges
that still own their Temples, and they will be contacted directly by the Committee
concerning this matter.
In addition to our responses to the many applications submitted to the
Committee for expenditures requiring Committee approval under section 1208 of
the California Masonic Code, your Committee members have made many
visitations to Lodges and Temple Associations, at their request, to counsel and
advise on Temple problems. They are pleased to offer their assitance throughout
the year. Also, they are available at this Annual Communication to provide
assistance and information. Included in this report is a summary of all formal
actions taken by the Committee during the year and at this Annual Communication. They will be published in the Annual Proceedings.

REPORT OF MASONIC HISTORY COMMITTEE

special projects. If a committee's functions are by-passed, there can be little
doubt regarding the considered worth or current status of the group.
As chairman of the History Committee during this last year, I wrote many
letters, some of them in desperation. In addition, I took the following action:
l) I drove from Bakersfield to San Francisco and discussed our situation with
our Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary.
2) I read the file on this Committee and found it disappointing. The
information I needed was not there.
3) I utilized a suggestion which emerged from the discussion with our Grand
Officers and assigned each of my Committee members the task of finding
a logical candidate for "Who's Who in California Masonry." This
assignment could enable each member to make a significant
contribition - if he had the dedication to do so-with virtually no expense
to himself.
4) I drafted a suggested set of guidelines for the future operation of this
Committee, sending our Grand Secretary and Junior Grand Warden each a
copy. Our Grand Secretary responded warmly and graciously, as I knew
he would.
5) I requested a more adequate budget for the next Masonic year.
While this Committee has not accomplished as much as we would have liked,
we have emerged from the total lethargy of only a few months ago. Now that my
term is over, I shall make myself available to the new Chairman and give him the
benefit of my brief experience. If he desires it, my successor will have
knowledge that I had to search for. He will know something of the budgetary
limitations. He will have a working set of guidelines to start his term and a
continuous program, if he and his Committee desire it.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:

Unlike some of the other such groups, the Masonic History Committee has no
continuous program. In fact, I had difficulty discovering its purposes. This has
been disconcerting, especially since I felt well-prepared to serve with this group.
After all, I worked six years with two other Grand Lodge Committees, have been
a Mason for more than thirty-four years, and I am a Past Master with a college
degree in history. By rule of thumb logic, the Committee was a natural, but my
qualifications appeared to be inadequate. Fortunately, our Grand Secretary
patiently explained the Masonic facts of life. There were, he told me, no
guidelines by which we were to function, no established program and virtually no
budget. Tersely stated, the Masonic History Committee appeared to be defunct.
Somewhat staggered by this, we gamely attempted to launch a program by
mail. I think we can claim a modicum of success, but it has not been easy. In
fact, this assignment has been both frustrating and discouraging. Correcting the
conditions which caused my frustration was a primary objective.
It is axiomatic that Lodge participation should gratify, at least to some degree,
the needs of the member. Such activity can only be satisfying if what one is doing
is regarded as important by those whom he serves. As Shakespeare might have
said, "There's the rub."
We recognize that Masonry in this Jurisdiction has many great strengths.
Unfortunately, our organization also harbors weaknesses, a few nebulous values,
and a lack of commitment in some instances. For example, our Grand Lodge
Committee system offers the promise of reward-participation in worthwile
endeavor by the many able, dedicated individuals within our Grand Lodge
Jurisdiction. It offers opportunity to serve to those who have the personal
commitment to devote themselves to their Lodge and to the Grand Lodge
organization. Unfortunately, in some instances, that promise is an empty one.
How many of our Grand Lodge Committees are so clearly defined in terms of
purpose and function that a new chairman would have no difficulty in guiding its
destiny? How many have clear-cut objectives? When I took over, my Committee
was, at best, in a coma.
It is my belief that each group should have clear direction to guide the
chairman and the committee membership. Aimless endeavor is rarely fruitful and
may lead to conflict among groups, undermining the spirit of our institution. A
basic set of guidelines would help to insure unified and productive direction, and
it would help to spell out minimum accomplishment. In addition, each new
chairman needs to be apprised of special problems, budgetary limitations and
procedures, and the past history of the group. Without such orientation, maximum progress is impossible. Believe me, I know.
It should not be overlooked that basic rules of procedure can protect the
integrity of a committee against having its purposes emasculated. I am not
critical of the ad hoc group that researched the California Masonic history for the
Centennial Year; its members did a workman-like job. My point is that our Grand
Jurisdiction has a standing committee which logically should be assigned such

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

This Committee has reviewed and reported on the Proceedings of fifty-one
Grand Lodges during the year. Forty-three of these were Grand Lodges within
the United States. Eight were from without the U. S.
In accordance with instructions and agreement with the Grand Master and the
Elective Officers of the Grand Lodge of California these reports were submitted

185

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

to the Senior Grand Warden for distribution to those whom he thought might find
them of value.
The condition of Masonry in the world, as represented by these proceedings is
strong and healthy. All of the Grand Lodges are supporting youth groups in
various ways, including financial support in some cases. All of them have
programs of charity and benevolence. Many have homes for children and old
folks on which millions of dollars are spend each year.
Others have hospitals, scholarships, low cost housing units for older Masons,
choirs, Masonic music, group insurance and other activities.
Some concerns include membership, age at initiation, physical disability,
consolidations, publicity, and of course, Masonic work.
In general, membership is declining. Losses range from a few members up to
seven per-cent in one Jurisdiction. The average seems to be around two per-cent.
Some reports indicate a levelling off from higher losses in previous years. In a
few cases membership is increasing, notably in the southern states of the U.S.A.
South Carolina reports an all time high in total membership. The picture seems to
me much the same in our country and abroad. One recent study showed increases
in only seven of the 48 jurisdictions in the U.S.A.
Several states have lowered the age for initiation to 18 or 19. Some of these
report a substantial number of young men being initiated, such as twenty per year
or so. Many of these are related to DeMolay activities.
Many have also adopted some relaxation of physical disability. Alabama, for
example reports dispensations for 17 maimed candidates, and refusal to relax on
two. Others report 18, 19 or 20 relaxations. All have very specific regulations for
such candidates. A few have refused to relax either age or physical requirements.
Consolidations of Lodges have taken place in many Jurisdictions, sometimes
strengthening local Lodges, sometimes resulting in loss in total membership.
Very few Grand Jurisdictions report charters to new Lodges. Illinois has
undertaken a two year study of the special problems of metropolitan Lodges, but
reported no action on this matter.
Attention is being given to proper publicity in many places. This includes
publications, workshops on the subject, speaker's bureaus and discussion of what
is proper to be publicized. In general, proper publicity is being encouraged
almost everywhere.
Much attention is also being given to training Lodge Officers in the ritual and
in the management of Lodges. Some Grand Lodge Officers leave a sheet of hints
on Lodge working and procedures when they visit local Lodges. In some, Grand
Officers file evaluations of the results of their visits. Several have well organized
leadership training programs. In Minnesota, for example, this program is in its
seventh year.
In some Jurisdictions the Grand Master sends letters to all Brothers who are
not paying their dues, trying to reduce suspensions. In others the Grand Master
sends letters to newly initiated Brothers, or newly raised Brothers.
Among others, Pennsylvania publishes forms for making bequests. Texas is
considering the formation of Spanish-speaking Lodges. Ohio made a two year
study of Prince Hall Masonry, reporting many activities quite similar to our own,
and that the origin of the organization was regular and legitimate.

These are a few of the activities that seem most unusual, or most noteworthy.
Illinois publishes some 75 pages of reports from other jurisdictions. On reviewing them I find much that is routine, and do not think that such a report would be
worthwhile for California. This is a very brief summary of many hundreds of
pages of proceedings.

Respectfully submitted,
J. WILSON GETSINGER, Chairman

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
COLUMBIA MASONIC TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The Columbia Temple Committee met twice during the past year.
At each meeting the Committee made a complete inspection of the building
and its facilities to insure that it is properly maintained. At the November
meeting it was quite evident that the woodwork around the windows and display
alcove was in need of paint. Being a dry fall the painting was completed before
the rains and prevented further erosion. The Committee has also instituted a
maintenance program covering several years to insure adequate maintenance on a
planned schedule.
The State Park Service count is 400,000 new visitors to the Park each year. It
is important with this amount of public exposure to display our facilities as a
credit to the Fraternity.
This being the Bicentennial Year and two movies being made in the Park the
count will be even higher. Our Temple represents a very important contribution
to the early days of the Mother Lode and Free Masonry in general.
During the year twenty-one (21) Lodges visited the Temple and conferred
degrees. Also the Stockton Scottish Rite and Royal Arch Masons used the
Temple.
The Committee wishes to thank the Grand Secretary, Edward H. Siems, and
his staff for their assistance this past year.

COMMITTEE ON TRAVEL ALLOWANCES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Travel Allowances submits the following report covering
the 127th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to Travel Allowance are the Master, or in his absence, the
ranking Warden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly Elected
Representative in accordance with Section 1148, California Masonic Code. Past
Grand Masters, not on Committees, will be reimbursed as provided in Section
1150, California Masonic Code. When a Master or Warden from the same Lodge
are present at an Annual Communication, and one of said Officers serves on a
Grand Lodge Committee entitled to travel and expense reimbursement, he shall
be reimbursed accordingly; the other Officer shall receive reimbursement under
Section 1148a, California Masonic Code, as the Officer representing his Lodge
on the floor of Grand Lodge.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San Francisco
has been taken from the published records of the California State Automobile
Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii to San Francisco has
been taken from the published reports of air lines, in accordance with Section
1148, California Masonic Code. No compensation is allowed to members from
San Francisco or the immediate vicinity. Compensation of members from the
State of California has been computed on the basis of eleven (11) cents per mile,
the rate fixed by the Committee on Finance. Compensation of the members from
the State of Hawaii has been figured on the basis of published first class
round-trip air rates of regularly scheduled major air lines, from Honolulu to San
Francisco, plus inter-island air fare to Honolulu, when necessary.

REPORT OF
COMMITTEE ON COMMERCIALISM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Commercialism submits herewith its report for the Masonic
Year 1976.
I
UNAUTHORIZED USE OF SQUARE & COMPASS

The chronic problem confronting the Committee is the unauthorized use ?f the
Square and Compass. This symbol is registered with the ~e~retary of Stat~ ~n the
name of the Grand Lodge. Its use by anyone else is proh1b1ted by both civil and
criminal laws.
The Committee has in most instances been able to obtain an agreement by the
errant user of the symbol to refrain from further use. The Brethren who print the
symbol on their checks or cards do so because of their pride in Masonry. Once
• informed of the misuse of the symbol they cease immediately.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Many printing companies advertise the Square and Compass with the letter
"G" as a symbol meaning "General Engineering." The Committee is attempting to contact all printing firms and advise them that the use of the symbol is a
violation of California Civil and Criminal laws.
The Committee at its annual meeting considered the use of the ''Square &
Compass" with the letter "G" by other organizations_ We are all aware that
ot?er organizations "openly and notoriously" use the "Square and Compas"
with the letter "G." This insignia is registered in the name of and is the sole
property of the Grand Lodge. The Committee is of the opinion that if some steps
~e. ~ot taken to curtail the use of the symbol by other organizations, we are
mv1tmg the permanent loss of the sole and exclusive use of the symbol.

IV

188

II
COMMERCIAL VENTURES

Throu~hout the past few years the Committee has been called upon to review
co~erc1al vent~res ~roposed by Lodges and Concordant Bodies. In one particu-

lar mstance the identical venture of a Lodge was criticized yet approved for a
concord~t body . Members of multiple bodies should distinguish between

commercial ventures proposed by Lodges and concordant bodies.
C.M.C. Section 333 states, in part:
'' . . . no lodge shall sponsor any collateral financial financial
undertaking . . . . "
The Appendix, on page 81, states:
'' . . . no organization shall engage in any project which is unethical
'
misleading, fraudulent or illegal.''
Simply stated, a Lodge may not sponsor any commercial venture, while a
concordant body may. However, a Concordant Body may not solicit the public,
unless all proceeds go to charity.

189

PROPOSED COMMERCIALISM MANUAL

Most of the Committee• s energies the past two years have been exerted toward
the formulation of an up-to-date Manual on Commercialism. Several revisions
have been completed, and the last revision has been intensely reviewed by the
Past Grand Masters as well as others. Because of several drastic changes,
including one that is almost identical to Resolution No. 11 submitted for your
vote this year, the Committee did not reach a unanimous agreement on the
proposal. Past Grand Masters Larry Dayton and Leo Anderson have reviewed the
proposed Manual in depth and have offered various criticisms and suggestions
which, in the final analysis, have caused the Committee to withdraw the proposal
from consideration at this· Communication. While this delays much-needed
action in this area for an additional year, a premature proposal would aggravate
the problems sought to be solved.
The Committee further recommends that the proposed Manual heretofore
submitted to Grand Lodge be referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence,
Policy & General Purposes, Youth Activities and all other appropriate committees for their review and submission to the next Grand Lodge Communication for
adoption.
The Committee appreciates the helpful cooperation of the Grand Master, the
Grand Secretary and the other Grand Lodge Officers.
It has been a distinct pleasure and honor to have served and worked with each
of them.
Respectfully submitted,

III
SHRINE GAMES

The only expressed purpose of this Committee is to review the Shrine Charity
games.
Over the past few years it has been our general observation that the Shrine
games, as a whole, have been attracting second-rate teams and players; the net
return to the charities is declining; and the cost of college level teams is
increasing. This has been allowed with the reasoning that "any return is better
·
than none. "
. I~ is the rec~mmendation of this Committee that an in-depth survey be made by
a Jomt-comffilttee of Grand Lodge and the various game committees to consider
ways and means to reverse this trend.

meeting took a lively part in the various deliberations, a fact which was noted

Full reports covering the Masonic Affiliated Youth Orders meeting, as well as

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE

During the past year your Committee has worked diligently to accomplish their
objectives by making many releases to the media and also by a large number of
personal contacts. We are finding that the media is developing an increasing
interest in our activities and projects. They desire more information about our
organization to permit them to more intelligently evaluate our particular goals.
To this end the Committee is now divided geographically into areas within the
Jurisdiction because public relations are often matters of personal contacts. This
system seems to be working very satisfactorily. It also appears to be the most
efficient plan from a cost standpoint.
We are aware that Freemasonry represents only the things that are good in our
society. There is presently, in the media, the beginning of a trend away from
negative journalism. If this continues, it is hoped that we can benefit from the
refreshing change and obtain more publicity for our great Fraternity. The result
should be greater interest by the uninitiated.

To the Most Worshipful Gand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The function of the Special Committee on Insurance is to assist and counsel the
Grand Master and Grand Secretary on such matters involving insurance protection of the property and exposures to financial risk of Grand Lodge and
Constituent Lodges and the responsibilities of their Officers.
The Committee endeavors to maintain a close liaison with the Grand Secretary
and his office and our insurance brokers and counselors and periodically review
the insurance program of policies in effect for adequacy of coverage and evaluate
requirements for any additional exposures for possible loss or risk.
It has come to our attention that certain sizable financial losses have been
sustained by Lodges in Masonic Jurisdictions of other States due to misappropriation of funds entrusted to Lodge Officers or Trustees which indicated a lack of
proper auditing and accounting control.
While to our knowledge, there has been no such unfortunate occurence in our
California Jurisdiction, it is the purpose of this report to stress the need for the
exercise of strict accounting procedures by the Officers and Trustees of our
Lodges for the preservation of their assets.
Another matter relating to Fire Insurance protection on Temple buildings
owned by Lodges has already been called to the attention- of our Lodges by the
article published in the September issue of the California Freemason. The
Committee wishes to point out the importance of proper supervision by those in
charge of handling the insurance for the Temple Associations so that a serious
fire loss will not jeopardize their finances.
Maintaining the proper amount of insurance to value in consideration of the
rising cost of labor and materials, architect's fees, contingent liability from
operation of building laws, cost of demolition and loss of rental income are all
matters that should be given due consideration for proper coverage.
Respectfully submitted,
ELMER C. GUNTHER, Chairman

HENRY W. SCHEUER

AFTER THE BICENTENNIAL, WHAT?
LAURENCE E. DAYTON, P.G.M.
Most Worshipful and Brethren:
I want to thank our Grand Master for granting me this time to address you on
the theme, "After the Bicentennial, What?"
We are approaching the end of the 200th year of American independence and
about to enter upon the third century of our national existence. It has been a time
to celebrate, and across the land we have celebrated mightily and in many ways.
This is as it should be.
But in the waning days of the anniversary it must be also a time for reflection,
a time to ask ourselves how well as a nation we have kept faith with the founders;
a time to re-orient ourselves to the principles they espoused, and to chart our
course into the future.
Two hundred years are a long time and our many achievements are indeed
worthy of note. But compared to the expanse of years that lie before us it is a
relatively short time. Stretching ahead into a far future yet beyond our ken is the
road we must travel. Will it be an up-grade or a down-grade? Will it lead us to the
heights of responsible freedom, or meek submission to all-powerful government?
A few days ago a United States Senator declared that "the people and the
government should be partners." What a profound misconception of what our
founders sought to establish! A partnership, as everyone knows, is formed by the
agreement of indepfndent parties, and his statement clearly implies that he
regards the government as independent of the people!
To the patriots there was no "and" between the people and the government. It
was "the people-thei r government. "
Let us never forget, nor suffer our leaders to forget, that the people of our
country are the source of power not the mere beneficiaries of its exercise. Nor
should we fail to see that it is not in distant capitols, but in the communities
where people live and work, rear and educate their children and manage their
common affairs that the destiny of America will be worked out. To use or
delegate their power wisely demands foresight and the application of individual
responsibility.
At a recent high school commencement one of the scholastic honor graduates
made a speech in which, among other things, he observed that ''the past is gone,
the future is not here, there is only the present." If this short term thinking is the
viewpoint of today's America we are in trouble.
While the problems of an immediate present gave impetus to the labors of the
dedicated Americans of 200 years ago, they were not working toward a transient
goal. Their vision was of the long future. It is not enough to be concerned only
with the immediate. The farther ahead we can see, the better. No point in time
can be isolated from the rest. For as inexorable in human affairs as in the natural
sciences is the law of cause and effect. It gives continuity and direction to human

201

·PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

experience and endeavor. By it past, present and future are bound together as
surely as are hydrogen and oxygen in the formula for water. Because the effect
may be separated in time from its cause, we should not fall into the error of
thinking the law is inoperative. However long the interval, however long the
account may be allowed to accumulate, it must be paid in full:
That's why history is so important. The founders knew this and searched
history for the clues that enabled them to avoid the pitfalls of the past as they set
about devising on the eastern shores of this continent a new concept for the
government of free men.
The common history of other nations may best be described by the geometric
figure called an arc ... the ascendence to a high point and a decline. This
experience has been so universal in both ancient and modem times that we say
"history repeats itself." If this is so, it is only because we have not learned its
lessons and go on making the same mistakes.
There is, however, a curve which is forever tending toward a straight line, but
no matter how far it may be extended, is still a curve.
I like to think that this curve rather than the arc symbolizes the possibilities of
America's future-our country's higher destiny.
But to set this kind of a course, some things are needful.
A useful place must be found in our society for everyone to the limits of his
abilities . Only in this way may both he and the nation profit by his talents. In this
regard, our so-called welfare system is a kind of hoax, for it tends to reduce the
individual's incentive to develop his abilities and the opportunity to put them to
work.
·
It should be noted that the decline of Rome was marked by the support in
idleness of vast numbers of people while among the opulent luxury and license
were rampant.
In our anxiety to achieve a nebulous "equality" we must not substitute quotas
for competence.
We must realize that knowledge and skill are not enough. They may be used
for good or ill. A sound course dictated by wisdom is essential and it is only
when knowledge is wedded to understanding that wisdom is born.
Unstinting effort on the part of all of us is required. The wise King Solomon,
by tradition our first Grand Master said, "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do
it with thy might. "
In other words, put all you' ve got into it. "That's good enough" is not good
enough. Had the founders of our Republic succumbed to the notion "that's good
enough" there would be no Bicentennial for us to celebrate. They taught us by
their example that nothing is good enough which is not the best we can do .
Integrity must characterize our every act whether as followers or leaders . The
patriots pledged to the task before them their lives, their fortunes and their sacred
honor. Perhaps it is too much in these times to expect that kind of commitment
from those who would assume national leadership, but we are at least entitled to
expect integrity. The poet Wordsworth described his " Happy Warrior" as
"One who if he rise to station of command
Rises by open means and there will stand
On honorable terms or else retire

And in himself possess his own desire."
This should be our standard and required memory work for all who seek our
suffrage.
.
Finally, the pursuit of dollars must make way for the pursmt of excellence·
Only such a motive can join us together in a common dream of greatness and set
us on a true course toward the heights .
There will come a time when "America the Beautiful" will seem as appropriate to our national aspirations as the martial tenor of the "Star Spangled
Banner."
"O BEAUTIFUL FOR PATRIOTS' DREAM
THAT SEES BEYOND THE YEARS;
THINE ALABASTER CITIES GLEAM
UNDIMMED BY HUMAN TEARS .
AMERICA, AMERICA, GOD MEND THINE EVERY FLAW;
,,
CONFIRM THY SOUL IN SELF-CONTROL, THY LIBERTY IN LAW ·
Over such an America as it ascends into the long future, may the Stars and
Stripes forever wave!

EMERGENT RESOLUTION-YOUTH GROUPS
TO SOLICIT PUBLIC
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Masonic Youth Orders are being beset by the ever increasing
cost of operation attended by increases in Lodge room rentals, convention
registration fees, recreational activities, administrative supplies, etc., and are
expected to maintain fiscal responsibility, and
WHEREAS, the Masonic Youth Orders are finding it increasingly difficult to
raise funds due to competition from other organizations who are able to advertise
and sell to the general public, and
WHEREAS, the Masonic Youth Orders are prohibited by Sections 2054 and
20701 and the Regulations Governing Organizations Subject to the Jurisdiction of
the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California from soliciting the
general public and from advertising for fund raising activities, and
WHEREAS, the Masonic Youth Orders cannot compete on an equitable basis
with other organizations because of the very restrictive rules of commercialism
imposed upon them, and
WHEREAS, advertising and public fund solicitation will serve to generate
greater awareness of Masonically affiliated or sponsored youth organizations,
therefore,
BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Second sentence of Section 2054 be amended
to read: "Lodges and other Masonic organizations may hold picnics, outings,
circuses and other family gatherings of their members, families, and friends for
which tickets are sold, but there may not be any public solicitations of sales of
tickets to such affairs by other than the Masonic Youth Orders and pending
clarification and/or direction of the Committee on commercialism, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 20701 be repealed, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 2071 be added to read: "The
Masonic Youth Orders may advertise and solicit the general public for fund
raising activities within the bounds of propriety and that fair prices are charged,''
and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Regulations Governing Organizations
Subject to the Jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of

(1)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, we learn that the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution of the United States of America were developed and brought into being
mostly by members of the Masonic Fraternity. Those Brothers involved pledged
their lives, fortunes, and sacred honor in order to secure those honorable
objectives, and
WHEREAS, it is inconceivable that these ends may have been achieved if the
Brethren had been reitrained by a Grand Lodge rule or regulation that prohibited
any political activity, and
WHEREAS, it seems that the objectives of our Brethren of 200 years ago are
being corrupted or passed aside by political activities, some of which are
immoral, decadent or dishonest in intent or purpose;
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Grand Master shall appoint
a committee who shall investigate this matter. They may recommend that the
Fraternity may support worthy causes or oppose unworthy causes which may
affect the government of the United States of America, or of the State of
California. If revision of the C.M.C. is required, they may so recommend. They
shall make a report at the 1977 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.

HAROLD s. JOHNSON, P.M. No. 454

Referred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 1 proposes that the Grand Master appoint a committee to
investigate the possibility of this Grand Lodge adopting positions of support or

206

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

opposition in political matters affecting the government of the United States of
America or of the State of California. The proposal implies that revision of the
California Masonic Code should be made to accommodate such actions if
required.
The Constitution of the Grand Lodge of California is the basic document from
which the structure and the powers of this Grand Lodge are derived. Rarely are
any provisions of this constitution amended. This is because the provisions in our
constitution are fundamental to Freemasonry in California. Our ordinances are
the regulations which we have adopted under authority of our constitution, and
they are amended or added to from time to time as conditions change or needs
arise.
Article III, Section 102, of the Constitution applies directly to the intent
contained in Resolution No. 1. This section reads as follows:
Section 102 Politics and Religion. The Grand Lodge and constituent Lodges
shall not intercede, interfere or voice an opinion with regard to domestic or
foreign, political or religious matters. Its members may represent all shades of
political and religious opinions, but when they are assembled in constituent or
Grand Lodge, they cannot so much as discuss such opinions. It is recognized
and expected that each Mason in this jurisdiction be a good citizen and that he
have a belief in God and a future existence and as an individual he conduct
himself accordingly. The Grand Lodge and constituent Lodges have their own
proper objectives and purposes, and those must be considered to the absolute
exclusion of all others, and particularly of such as would arouse contention and
confusion.

PAY OF REPRESENTATIVES ATTENDING
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that this section of
our Constitution is completely proper and completely right. We believe that any
deviation from the policy so clearly enunciated in Section 102 could lead to great
trouble for this Grand Lodge and its constituent Lodges. Resolution No. 1 both
suggests and proposes deviation, and, if enacted, would most assuredly lead to
contention and confusion.
The proposers infer that the Brethren may be restrained by Grand Lodge rules
or regulations prohibiting political activity. No such restraint exists. Every
Mason is free to participate as a citizen in whatever manner and for whatever
cause he may choose. Actually this Grand Lodge encourages the members of our
Fraternity to be good citizens, and obviously participation in political activity is a
part of good citizenship.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recognizes and appreciates
the concern of the proposers of Resolution No. 1, but it is the unanimous and
solid belief of the committee that what is proposed in Resolution No. 1 qm only
lead to dangerous disharmony among the Brethren.
I therefore move the adoption of Resolution No. 1 and your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes both recommends and urges a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.
