Respectfully submitted,
ORAN 0. BRIDGES, P.M. No. 776

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and on
Finance.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 4 seeks to amend our California Masonic Code to provide not
only a transportation allowance to a Lodge Representative attending an Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge (which provision is presently in effect) but also
to reimburse such Representative for all necessary expenses in attending an
Annual Communication.
The policy of our Grand Lodge as is evidenced from (Old Sections 174 and
176) now Sections 1148 and 1150 of the California Masonic Code, 2nd Edition
provides for (I) reimbursement of travel expenses for Officers or Representatives
of the Lodges, (2) reimbursement of travel expenses and necessary expenses for
Grand Officers, Committeemen and Inspectors and (3) only reimbursement of
travel expenses for Past Grand Lodge Officers who are not Committeemen.
The purpose of this demarcation is self-evident. Those who are Grand Lodge
Officers, Committeemen and Inspectors are beholden to Grand Lodge and all of
the Lodges of this Jurisdiction and therefore represent the entire Jurisdiction not
an individual Lodge. As for the Lodge Officers or Representatives, they are only
responsible to their respective Lodges. We are all aware of our Stated Meetings
where the Master seeks and obtains the opinion of the members of his Lodge and
is directed to vote on resolutions according to the will of the majority members of
his Lodge.
To amend our Regulations to make Officers or Representatives of Lodges
reimbursable for expenses at an Annual Communication relegates that person to a
greater responsibility to the Grand Lodge than to his individual Lodge. This is
contrary to our governmental process and intent of Grand Lodge. The individual
Lodge must share in the financial responsibility.
A prime purpose of Section ~ 148 is to encourage the attendance of a Lodge
Officer or Representative at Grand Lodge; further than that no other financial
responsibility is necessary or proper.

The Finance Committee:
At the 1975 Annual Communication, the Committee on Finance reported in
part: "We are presently engaged in a study of the pay of members attending
Grand Lodge, but we are not prepared to make recommendation at this time."
Resolution No. 4, which has been referred to the Committee on Finance, is, in
fact, an outgrowth of this study and is authored by a member of our Committee.
In order to properly evaluate this resolution, it is necessary to recall certain
historical facts. At the 1966 Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, the
recommendation of then Grand Master Myron E. Smith was adopted that "the
Finance Committee of the Grand Lodge be requested to make a comprehensive
study and review the whole subject of expenditures of Lodge funds and Grand
Lodge funds . . . and to submit its findings and recommendations at the Next
Annual Communication.''
During the two years which followed, first the Committee on Finance, and
later the Special Fin~nce Study Committee appointed in 1967, made a comprehensive study of the expenditure of funds, including the "pay of members"
attending the Annual Communication and also the matter of reimbursement of
Grand Lodge Officers and Committeemen for necessary travel expenses incurred
in the discharge of their duties. The study was completed and the findings
presented to the 1968 Annual Communication. In the Grand Master's Report at
that Communication, then Grand Master Eugene S. Hopp recommended that the
report of the Special Finance Study Committee be adopted in principle. The
Grand Lodge adopted Grand Master Hopp's recommendation, and thus was
established the principle of necessary travel expense reimbursement for Officers,
Inspectors and Committmen engaged in Grand Lodge business.
In 1969, in the interest of equity and expense control, provision was made for
annually setting certain maximum allowable reimbursement for lodging and meal
expense in the San Francisco area while attending the Annual Communication.
At the 1974 Annual Communication then Grand Master Raymond A. Ebbage
again brought up the reimbursement of travel expenses in his message to the
Grand Lodge. He stated:
' 'When one of our dedicated members spends time and money in the service of
his Brethren, he should not be asked to shoulder the entire burden while the
inactive ·members sit idly by. We should all be willing to share, at least

211

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

financially, in the costs incurred for such services . I recommend that future
standards of reimbursement be adequate to meet those expenditures . This policy
could result in increased dues or assessments, but the results will generally far
outweigh the cost."
His recommendation initiated further study by the Committee on Finance
resulting, first, in the 1975 revision of the automobile mileage allowance for
persons using their personal automobiles on Grand Lodge business, and secondly, in Resolution No. 4 which is being considered by you today . Against this
historical background, let us then examine the provisions of Resolution No. 4.
A substantial number of the Lodge representatives attending this Communication are shouldering their entire expense burden; others receive partial assistance
through the present "mileage allowance;" while still others may receive full
reimbursement through their respective Lodges.
The most compelling reason for the adoption of Resolution No. 4 is the need,
in our opinion, to minimize the personal expense burden sustained by a Lodge
Officer in attending the Annual Communication and thus promote an increase in
the attendance and resultant participation of Lodge representatives in conducting
the business of this Grand Lodge.
This Grand Lodge has for many years made use of a method to partially
assume the expenses of a representative attending the Annual Communication .
The method whereby checks are prepared on the basis of computed mileage
multiplied by an arbitrary rate per mile is antiquated, and of greater importance,
has no reference to any level of actual cost. In fact, there is a notable inequality in
the present method for the reason that most representatives in our Southern
Districts receive in their checks an amount significantly in excess of their actual
transportation costs, while representatives from other areas do not share in this
largesse.
This resolution, therefore, proposes that the present fair and equitable method
of reimbursing Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors and Committeemen-a principle adopted by this Grand Lodge in 1968-be now extended to include the
principal representative of Constituent Lodges. It will serve to remove the
obstacle to Grand Lodge attendance for the Brother whose personal financial
means might not otherwise enable him to become involved. It will also strongly
encourage Masters to remain in attendance the full duration of the Annual
Communication rather than limit their participation to one or two days.
Obviously, this program of more equitable expense reimbursement for Lodge
representatives will involve increased cost to Grand Lodge and must be paid for .
The usual and only method we have of providing funds is through the per capita
assessment. Your Committee on Finance has made a study, using what we
believe to be reasonable assumptions, which indicates that an additional 35 cents
would need to be added to the present per capita for this purpose. Your
consideration of this resolution must necessarily keep in mind this increase in the
per capita, but you must also remember that it should then no longer be necessary
for Constituent Lodges to draw on their Lodge funds to financially assist their
Master when he comes to the Annual Communication. Thus, to a large degree,
the financial impact of Resolution No. 4 on many Lodges will not represent a
significant increase in total expenditures, but will largely be a transfer of money

from one pocket to another. Let us again recall the emphasis in 1974 of then
Grand Master Ebbage that establishing just and fair standards of travel expense
reimbursement may result in increased assessment~. but the beneficial results
will generally far outweigh the cost.
Therefore, your Committee on Finance strongly recommends a "Yes" vote on
Resolution No. 4.

Masonic Service Bureaus, the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California and such

Retirement Plan Committee, in accordance with the Employees Retirement

TEMPLE ALTERATIONS -INCREASE
DISCRETIONARY EXPENDITURES TO $5000.00
(6)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, Section 199(3) of the California Masonic Code requires prior
approval of the Committee on Lodge Financing to expend more than $2,500.00
to erect or alter a 'Masonic Temple; and
WHEREAS, that limitation has existed for more than twenty years; and
WHEREAS, in the present economy, many alterations of an emergency nature
require expenditures exceeding the present limitation; and
WHEREAS, inherent in existing Masonic Law is the requirement that such
expenditures be made from funds on hand unless prior approval of the Committee
is had;
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that Section 199(3) of the California
Masonic Code be amended to substitute the figures $5,000.00 for the present
figures $2,500.00.
Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 6 proposes to change Section 1208 (old Section 199 (3) of the
C.M.C. which reads, "No Lodge, temple association, Lodge trustees, committee, association, partnership or corporation, representing itself as Masonic in
character or operating for the benefit of a Masonic Lodge or Lodges, Masonry or
Masons, shall undertake any plan, scheme, project or method whereby:
1. Real property is to be purchased, or
2. Leased for more than three years, or
3. A Masonic temple is to be erected or altered whereby the total expenditure
will exceed the sum of $2,500.00 without first obtaining the written
approval of the Committee on Lodge Financing."
Section 199 (3) was adopted in 1954.
This Resolution proposes to change Section 1208 (old Section 199 (3)) by
increasing the limitation to $5,000.00 from $2,500.00 for expenditures that may
be made without written approval because, due to the present economy, many
alterations of an emergency nature require expenditures in excess of the present
limitation.
It is the opinion of the Committee that expenditures of $5,000.00 or less,
should not require the written approval of the Committee on Lodge Financing.
Inflation, alone, prescribes the propriety of this proposal.
Your Committee supports the proposal contained in Resolution No. 6.
I therefore move the adoption of Resolution No. 6 and your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 9 proposes to amend Section 2046, (old Section 324, subparagraph e) of our California Masonic Code and allow Lodges to hold meetings
in certain places out of doors.
If more interest and participation in Freemasonry can be generated by this
measure and selected sites can be duly and properly tiled , your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes believes that this legislation would be beneficial to
our Institution.
I therefore move the adoption of this resolution and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Committee on Ritual:
Resolution No . 9 as initially reviewed by the Ritual Committee brought forth
several areas of concern such as security, application of Ritual and propriety.
In our opinion adequate security in view of modem technology would be very
difficult if not practically impossible to assure in all but a few selected areas.
Outdoor meetings are not new. Open-air meetings have been held in the past in
various locations in our Jurisdiction. Unfortunately, such meetings had to be
discontinued because of breaches of security and propriety.
In the absence Qf regulations to govern the conduct of open air meetings, the
Committee feels that the recurrence of such breaches are possible. However,
after thorough discussion with the proposers of the Resolution and further
deliberations by the Committee, a set of rules and guidelines have been
established which we believe will properly assure secrecy, proper application of
ritual and propriety.
With this assurance and being fully desirous of establishing programs which
could promote increased interest and activity within Masonry, we of the
Committee on Ritual concur with the Policy and General Purposes Committee in
their recommendation of a "Yes" vote.

immediately, and of itself, terminate his membership in all Lodges in this

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 13 proposes to clarify a possible ambiguity concerning the
suspension or expulsion of a multiple member. Sec. 2402 (432(6)). The resolution would first define automatic suspensions and expulsions to take place only if
the initiating Lodge causing the suspension or expulsion was a Lodge within the
Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California. It further provides that if the
initiating Lodge were outside the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of the State of
California, then the Master of the California Lodge shall cause such action to be

226

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

taken by the California Lodge or that charges be preferred against the multiple
member as the facts warrant under the laws of Grand Lodge of California.
The proponent of the resolution points out that the possible ambiguity in the
current law could result in a suspension or expulsion of a member of a Lodge
within the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California for conduct or activities
which may not be compensible by the laws of the Grand Lodge of California.
This would obviously result in an inequitable application of the laws of the Grand
Lodge of California.
I , therefore, move the adoption of this resolution and your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes recommends a " Yes" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence :
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution has been referred,
reports as follows:
After discussing with the proponent, his intent and proposal, your Committee

REDUCE MINIMUM AGE LIMIT
(15)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, a person eighteen (18) years old is now of the age of majority
under State and Federal laws, and
WHEREAS, the age of majority for Masonic purposes should conform to the
law of the land, and
WHEREAS, Grand Jurisdictions which have lowered to eighteen (18) the age
bf eligibility to apply for the degrees of Masonry have experienced an increase in
petitions from young men in their twenties, and
WHEREAS, it is desirable that there be an infusion of young men in the
Lodges of this Grand Jurisdiction,
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that a new section be added to the
California Masonic Code to read as follows:

231

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Section 511.1. A male person who has reached the age of eighteen (18) years
shall be deemed a man for the purpose of petitioning for the degrees of
Masonry.''
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED , that Section 51 l(a) of the California Masonic
Code be deleted.

accomplished in reducing the age to 18? Is it logical that a young man, 21 years
of age, would apply for the degrees merely on the basis that the age limit had
been reduced to 18?
Your Committee is also deeply concerned with the effect this resolution would
have on the Order of DeMolay and consideration must be given to this concern.
A DeMolay remains such until his twenty-first birthday. If he became a Master
Mason at the age of 18, would he then lose his interest and cease being active in
DeMolay? If so, this would create a very serious negative effect, because
DeMolay survives on the continued support and the efforts of these young men
until they arrive at the age of twenty-one.
If this Grand Lodge adopts any legislation that would, or could in any way ,
seriously undermine the Order of DeMolay, then we have failed in fulfilling our
duty and our obligation to these young men who may become Master Masons at
the age of 21 . DeMolay looks to the Grand Lodge of California, not only for our
support, but for our protection from anything that could destroy their efforts.
Your Committee does not subscribe to the theory that our Fraternity should be
evaluated or judged on the size of our membership. We believe that quality is
always preferable to quantity.
To become a Master Mason is a rare privilege and no civil law can change that
fact. Freemasonry is a unique Fraternity in that we seek no man to take our
degrees; that they must come to us of their own free will. Should Freemasonry
become like every other fraternity, lowering its standards for the sake of
increasing membership? We think not. To change our law merely for increasing
membership serves no useful purpose. We should maintain our standards
regardless of that which may appear expedient at the moment.
California Freemasonry has set a standard that is the envy of every Grand
Jurisdiction in the United States . Let us maintain and support our present policy
and our present philosophy- to accept good men and make them better men.
I move the adoption of Resolution No. 15 and your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

POSSESSION AND USE OF CIPHER RITUALS
(16)

Far more serious is another problem . There is a basic principle that all men are
presumed to know the law. If we require that instruction be given on one
particular prohibition, it could logically be argued by a Brother on trial or in
trouble for a violation for some other of our laws that he violated it because he
was ignorant of it. If special instruction is required that Brothers may not be
ignorant of one of our ordinances, his argument is logical.
Furthermore, we already have a provision contained in California Masonic
Code, Section 2530, Subsection 6, which makes it a duty of the Master of a
Lodge, "To carefully guard against any infraction, by the members of his Lodge,
of its own By-laws, of the Constitution or Regulations of the Grand Lodge, or of
the General Regulations of Masonry. ' ' This duty is further emphasized at the
installation of the Master when he is charged by the Installing Officer as follows :
" This book of Constitutions you are expected diligently to search and from
time to time to cause its contents to be read in your Lodge, that none may
remain ignorant of the precepts it enjoins, or of the ordinances which it
promulgates."
This places a duty on the Master to see that all precepts and ordinances are
known by all, whether Entered Apprentice, Affiliate or any other. To require that
one point only be given special emphasis would be contrary to the general rule .
There is one additional point. If this one point were now deemed to merit
special emphasis and be added to the Code, would another point arise next year
requiring the same action and so on?
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes, therefore, moves the adoption of the Resolution but recommends a " No" vote.

From the 197 l In-Depth Study Report:
"(A) Position favoring change:
In the letter of the appointment of this committee, the Most Worshipful Grand
Master Herbert A. Huebner requested the committee to make a thorough study of
the subject and to submit a report, containing its observations, conclusions, and
recommendations, and that the report should be full and fair. This would in our
opinion justify a thorough study of all phases of the subject.
Prior to meeting, various materials were submitted to the Committee for study.
Much information, not generally known to the average Mason, was contained in
the materials distributed. Among this materials, there was one paper called the
"Doctrine of the Perfect Youth," printed by the Masonic Service Association,
700 Tenth Street N.W., Washington I, D.C. The first edition was issued
December, 1937 and a revised edition was issued September 22, 1950. This
publication contained a summary of the procedures of handling physicallyhandicapped candidates of the 49 Grand Jurisdictions in the United States,
including the District of Columbia.
It was noted i1' this summary that, at that time, there were 42 Grand
Jurisdictions that did accept physically-handicapped persons using various procedures for accepting them.
Seven of the 49, including California still adhered to the strict rule of the
"Perfect Youth."
Of the 42 that were accepting applicants, 30 of them left the decision to the
discretion of the Lodge, l l were left up to the Grand Masters, and 2 were left up
to the Master of the Lodge to decide.
It was apparent that there were some irregularities in some of these procedures,
from the standpoint of the conferring of the degrees, and there was some
indication that they were straying from the ritual, especially as we know it in
California where we are accustomed to the highest quality ritual available
anywhere, and are desirous of keeping it that way.
There was one plan, however, adopted by the Grand Lodge of Indiana which
appears to have solved the problem and with certain variations we feel it could be
very applicable to our situation here in California.
In 1961-the Grand Lodge of Indiana passed legislation to create an Occasional Lodge to operate Under Dispensation, for the sole purpose of conferring
the degrees of Masonry upon Candidates of other Lodges who were under
physical handicaps, and whereby they were unable to literally conform to the
ritual.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Prior to this time Indiana had been accepting physically-handicapped candidates and each individual Lodge was conferring the degrees upon them, thus
more or less adapting their own ritual to the case at hand. This was not proving
satisfactory to those who wanted the ritual preserved, so they set out to find a
better way to accomplish the purpose without returning to the "Perfect Youth"
theory.
This was accomplished in the establishment of an Occasional Lodge Under
Dispensation named Bartimaeus Lodge in reference to blind Bartimacus receiving his sight and being made whole as stated in the New Testament, Ref: St.
Mark 10:46 through 10:52.
Although the name Bartimaeus may seem to some to have a significance to the
situation, it is not necessarily so and any applicable name would be appropriate.
Such as, Realization Lodge, Ritualistic Lodge or Occasional Lodge. For identification purposes we shall use the name Occasional Lodge Under Dispensation.
Although the mechanics of such a Lodge cannot be fully described in this
report we can consider most of the basic ideas.
The idea was conceived by a group of men who wanted to see the ritual
preserved, yet who wanted to allow the degrees of Masonry to be conferred upon
those who were physically handicapped, and, who were otherwise worthy and
well qualified.
To do this, they suggested the formation of a Lodge that would consist only of
''Blue Ribbon'' ritualists, who would meet occasionally solely for the purpose of
conferring the degrees of Masonry upon physically-handicapped candidates of
other Lodges. Those receiving the degrees were not made members of the
Occasional Lodge, but were members of the Lodge which they petitioned.
It must be remembered that this Occasional Lodge was not a Lodge to accept
physically-handicapped persons. Its only function was to confer the degrees upon
physically-handicapped candidates of other Lodges. In other words it performs a
speci.al function, to guarantee that the degrees are conferred upon physicallyhand1capped candidates, in a manner distinguished for its perfection.
Without further details as to the workings of this arrangement which we
consider highly commendable, we wish to summarize by offering the following
recommendations.
It is thought by those making this summary that legislation should be
introduced to establish the creation of a Special Lodge in the State of California
and Hawaii, for the sole purpose of conferring the degrees of Masonry upon
candidates of Constituent Lodges who are under physical handicaps whereby
they are unable to conform to the present ritual.
. The creation of such a Lodge, would by no means represent a change in policy
with respect to petitioners who are physically handicapped (except as it shall be
later stated). This would allow all present safeguards to be retained for the ritual,
and in addition, the Grand Lecturer and his staff would have the sole control over
the manner in which the degrees would be conferred.
Our recommendation would be to establish three such Lodges all of the same
name, and in the same manner, one in the North, one in the South and one in
Hawaii for the convenience of the officers and candidates.
. As her~tofore mentioned, thes.e Special Lodges would operate under Dispensation, havmg no charter, not ownmg property, nor having a vote in Grand Lodge,

and having no other powers except the sole purpose of conferring the degrees of
Masonry upon physically-handicapped candidates of constituent Lodges in this
Jurisdiction, all of which would be under direction of the Grand Lecturer.
It is recommended that the Grand Lecturer should appoint the officers of the
respective Special Lodges each year and before such officer may be installed he
must qualify himself before the Grand Lecturer or his appointee.
The above recommendations would, we feel, qualify for the proper conferring
of the degrees and would lend to the control and dignity appropriate to the
occasion.
In order to make this possible we would recommend certain changes in to
C.M.C. To wit:
l . That the physical qu_alifications of a person shall be no bar for application
if he is otherwise worthy and well qualified. Ever remembering that the
physical sufficiency of the applicant shall be left to the sound discretion of
the Lodge, and if elected, the degrees must be conferred by qualified
ritualists.
2. Sec. 511, is proposed to be amended to read:
An applicant for the degrees of Masonry must be a man; a believer in God
and a future existence; of moral conduct; capable of reading and writing;
of supporting himself and family; having no maim or defect in his mind or
body that may render him incapable of learning the art, and physically
able to conform substantially to what the several degrees respectively
require of him, provided however that if an applicant who is unable to
comply with the physical requirements by virtue of a physical disability or
disabilities, the application may be received and voted upon by the Lodge
in accordance with Sec. 512 (as proposed for amendment).
3. Sec. 512 Proposed to amend:
Before an applicant, who has a physical handicap, may apply for the
degrees, it will be necessary for him to appear before a special committee
of not less than 5, appointed by the Master of the Lodge to which he
wishes to make the application. This committee shall consist of not less
than two of the principal officers of the Lodge, and other members whom
the Master may appoint. The committee shall request that the proposed
applicant appear before them at the lodge hall in a private room suitable
for the occasion and with dignity, to view the extent of the proposed
applicant's disability and determine whether or not the proposed applicant
could substantially conform to the ritual. Upon conclusion of the interview if in the opinion of the committee, that the proposed applicant could
not substantially conform to the ritual it would be their duty to inform him
that he could not qualify and therefore, to relieve him of the possible
embarrassment of being rejected, would recommend that he not make an
application to the lodge.
If it was the opinion of the committee that the proposed applicant could
substantially qualify, they would advise him that if it was his decision to
proceed with an application that this preliminary investigation would in no
way be construed as a guarantee that he would be elected to receive the
degrees.

In substantiation of this, we would like to make certain references regarding
the above, i.e., the Landmarks.
LANDMARK 18. States only, quote, "The qualification of candidates for
initiation," unquote._ Note: No reference is made as to physical qualifications,
therefore no change is necessary.
LANDMARK 24. States that Masonry is: Quote, ''The foundation of a
speculative science upon an operative art, and the symbolic use and explanation
of ~h~ terms of that art, for the purpose of religious or moral teaching." Unquote.
This 1~ self-e~planatory and tends to refute the opinion that symbolism has no
place m our ntual . See C.M.C. Sec. 51 lJ for reference to symbolism. We must
reme!Ilber that we will now confer the second or third degree of Masonry upon a
candidate who may have suffered an accident after he has received his first
degree, thus employing symbolism or exemplification to do so. It seems rather
ambiguous that we could do this in one case and not in another.
LANDMARK 25. Quote, "The last and crowning landmark of all is, that
these landmarks can never be changed." Unquote.

which is inevitable, and must be recognized as such. Anything that can be, or has
been, established by man may also be altered by man.
The written laws, together with the landmarks, constitute the foundations of
Masonic law. The landmarks where applicable should not be changed, but where
they no longer exist due to our own change, i.e., from operative Masonry to
speculative Masonry, they are then not applicable to the art. And further that
there is nothing in the landmarks that prohibit us from accepting anyone who is
physically disqualified. It is only the old rules and regulations, practiced in the
early history of operative Masonry, that mention anything of not accepting a
perfect youth, or a man who is not of sound body, or a person that may have a
maim in his body. By reviewing all the written laws and regulations prior to
1721, we find that they are totally inconsistent with our present way of living and
it would be impossible to comply with them or even find a place for them in
todays society. It is mentioned in the C.M.C. on page 364, under Grand Lodge
Powers In General, that the Constitutions and Regulations of 1721 thereto may
be altered or amended by a Grand Lodge; they, however, remain in force until so
amended or changed by positive enactment of the Grand Lodge. We therefore,
repeat, that it is the old written laws and regulations (and which it is stated, can
be repealed or changed) that is causing some of the minds to cling to the belief
that a man must be of sound limb and body to be accepted into speculative
Masonry.
We also feel that by making a true analysis of this report, which is backed up
with documented evidence to support it and other evidence gained by men in
their travels and the fact that only seven out of the 49 Grand Jurisdictions in the
United States, including California, still adhere to the strict rule of the perfect
youth, that we will find it difficult to bring forth logical evidence that we should
not consider a change in California procedures for the acceptance of physicallyhandicapped perscms if otherwise qualified.
It is therefore, our strong desire and recommendation that further consideration
be given to this matter based upon the information submitted in this report. Ever
remembering that physical sufficiency of the applicant shall be left to the sound
discretion of the Lodge, and that the degrees would be conferred by "Blue
Ribbon" ritualists.
We would like to close this report with the final recommendation that the

"(B) Position-Against Change
At the 1970 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes moved "that this Grand Lodge instruct the
incoming Grand Master to appoint a special commission on Physical Qualifications for the purpose of conducting an in-depth study on the entire matter of
physical requirements for admission to Masonry in this Jurisdiction and with the
instruction to report in detail to this Grand Lodge when its work is completed,
and, if possible, to do so at the 1971 Annual Communication." The motion was

carried and the Grand Master, Most Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner, appointed
your Committee, stating "I desire this Committee to make a thorough study, and
to submit a report containing its observations, conclusions and recommendations. It shall be full and fair, so that the Grand Lodge may intelligently act upon
the question."
Your Committee has reviewed a wealth of material, including our own
proceedings, a copy of the Masonic Service Association booklet entitled "Doctrine of the Perfect Youth,'' and reviewed many of the physical requirements of
other Grand Jurisdictions, including the Grand Lodge of Minnesota as published
in the Proceedings of Educational Lodge No. 1002 ofMinneapolish; the report of
Indiana by its Grand Secretary; and reports from the Grand Lodges of Louisiana
and North Carolina; and the publication of the Philalethes Society, which
contains reports of discussions taking place on the subject of Physical Qualifications at the annual meeting of the Society in Washington, D.C. February 19,
1971.
At a meeting of this Committee, a vote was taken as to those favoring a change
in the physical requirements necessitating a change in ritual; the results were five
in favor and five against. Those favoring a change in the requirements have
determined to present a separate report . This report is made by the Chairman and
those recommending no change in the physical requirements.
The present regulations governing physical qualifications in California are
contained in sections 511 and 512 of the California Masonic Code.

that it was not within the province of the Grand Master or of the Grand Lodge to
remove this ancient landmark. This was before Dr. Albert Mackey formulated
his statement of 25 Landmarks.
The position of the Grand Lodge itself was first declared in 1864, when it
adopted the report of its Committee on Jurisprudence, in answer to the question,
"Do the ancient charges require the applicant for the mysteries of Masonry to be
physically perfect, and if not, what degree of dismemberment or deformity shall
exclude him?" (Proceedings of 1864, pp. 363-4)
That report, in its own words went for the answer to the "foundation-the
landmarks and ancient charges." After referring to the 18th Landmark as given
by Dr. Mackey, the report quoted the ancient charges approved by the Grand
Lodge of England in 1722: "No Master should take an apprentice ... unless he
be a perfect youth, having no maim or defect in his body that may render him
incapable of learning the art .. .. "They concluded that these, "taken together,
form a part of the body of Masonry, in which we are agreed that no man or body
of men can make innovations." (Please note that in 1722 Masonry was
speculative, not operative.)
The question to be determined, the 1864 report stated, is as to the proper
interpretation of the language used in the landmark and the charge quoted. To
explain the landmark and charge, they referred to the 5th article of the Old York
Constitutions of 926: ''A candidate must be without blemish and have the full
and proper use of his limbs, for a maimed man can do the Craft no good;" to the
Regulations of 1663: "No person shall herafter be accepted as a Freemason but
such as are of able body;" and to the Ancient Charges at Makings, at about the
year 1686: "That he be made able in all degrees . . . and that he have his right
limbs as a man ought to have." The report then stated that "one who has lost any
of those members, or any of those senses which are brought into use and required
by the necessities of the work of the lodge, would have such 'maim or defect in
his body as to render him incapable of learning the art,' and he could not be said
to 'have his right limbs as a man ought to have'."
The Committee disagreed with Dr. Mackey's view that absolute perfection
was required, but concluded ''that it is a violation of Masonic usage to admit any
man who is incapable of complying literally with what is required of him in
passing through the ceremonies of each degree."
The Grand Lodge thereupon adopted the express rule that

Sec. 511. Moral and Physical Qualifications. An applicant for the degrees
of Masonry must be a man; no woman nor eunuch; free born, being neither a
slave nor the son of a bond woman; a believer in God and a future existence; of
moral conduct; capable of reading and writing; having no maim or defect in his
body that may render him incapable of learning the art, and physically able to
conform substantially to what the several degrees respectively require of him.
Sec . 512. Sound Discretion Required. The question as to the physical
sufficiency of the applicant is left to the sound discretion of the Lodge. When
the applicant is unable to comply literally with the physical requirements, the
Master shall state the nature and extent of his disabilities to the Lodge before
ballot is taken.
There has never been any method of making Masons in this jurisdiction except
by the candidate individually receiving the degrees in strict accordance with the
ritual adopted by Grand Lodge. According to section 554 of the C.M.C., "each
degree conferred . . . in this jurisdiction must be in conformity with the ritual
now taught by the Grand Lecturer and recognized by the Grand Lodge, and such
must be adhered to by all Lodges and Masons in this jurisdiction."
Obviously, to accommodate disabled or deformed candidates, it would require
a complete change of ritual, indeed many different varieties of ritual, depending
upon the nature and extent of the disability or deformity. There could be no
uniformity of ritual.
Let us review the history of the rule in California.
The matter of physical qualifications was first discussed in this jurisdiction by
Grand Master William H. Howard in May, 1855, when he stated to Grand Lodge

243

"The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man . . . not
deformed or dismembered, but hale and sound in his physical conformation,
having his right limbs as a man ought to have; and be able to conform literally
to what the several degrees respectively require of him."
This rule was reaffirmed in 1872 (1872:556) and at various other times,
whenever the question was raised. (1894:767; 1897:234)
In 1900 the rule as to physical qualifications was again reviewed by the
Committee on Jurisprudence, which explained that in 1864 the Jurisprudence
Committee had endorsed the view that the perfection required by the Ancient
Charges approved in 1722 was simply that the candidate should have no maim or
defect that might render him incapable of learning the art, and that if he had no

245

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

such maim or defect, then he was a "perfect youth" for all the purposes of
Masonry and therefore eligible. They then recommended, and Grand Lodge
adopted, an amendment of the rule to read as follows:

that as far back as our written record goes, the qualification of candidates has
been a part of our landmarks, and had in its inception, or in its later history, no
connection with the occupation of the operative Mason.
The report expressly stated that ''This Grand Lodge has recognized and is
committed to twenty-five landmarks, of which the eighteenth is 'the qualification
of candidates for admission' ; and that under our Constitution the power of the
Grand Lodge is limited 'by a strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks of the
Order'; and that among the Ancient Charges and Regulations to which a Master
must submit before installation is the following: 'You admit that it is not in the
power of any man or body of men to make innovations in the body of Masonry.'
The landmarks being unrepealable must ever continue in force, and constitute the
unwritten law of Masonry." The report reviewed the Old Charges and Regulations as to physical ability and recommended that pending resolutions having for
their purpose a change in our law be not adopted. Grand Lodge voted to follow
this recommendation and adopted the Committee report. (1946: 194-197)
Subsequent resolutions having for their purpose the modification of the rule on
physical qualifications have been voted dow~. In 1962, Grand Master Guy B.
Mize, on recommendation of the Committee on Jurisprudence, concurred in by
the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on Ritual, declared a
resolution purporting to rescind the physical requirements to be contrary to the
landmarks of Masonry and declared it rejected. (1962:263)
In 1963 (1963:pp. 298-300), the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
summarized in its report the reasons for rejection of physical qualfication
changes which had been presented virtually every year for more than a decade. It
is worth reproducing here:
"Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes ... (has considered the
proposals to eliminate the requirements of physical qualification) ... without
emotion and only ftom the standpoint of what, in our opinion, would be good for
Masonry.
"Masonry selects its candidates and admits them only after careful investigation and a unanimous ballot. No one has a right to become a Mason. It is a
privilege granted to a comparatively small number.
"To begin with, we exclude half of the human race . No woman can become a
Mason. (It might be noted parenthetically that a 14,000 member men's club in
California, formed solely for the purpose of 'getting the facts ,' having been
threatened with suit for failure to admit women, while receiving a tax-exempt
status, has now permitted women to become members). Half of the remainder of
· the population is likewise excluded, namely any one under the required age of 21
years. (Again we insert the question of this age restriction against the background
of the recently granted vote to 18-year-olds.)
"In California, for more than one hundred years, we have adhered to the
regulation that no one having a maim or defect in his body that may render him
incapable of learning the art and physically unable to conform to what the several
degrees respectively require of him, can become a Mason.
''The physical requirements of qualification of candidates for the degrees of
Masonry are probably as old as Masonry itself. They are a survival of Operative

244

' 'The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man . . . having no
maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable of learning the art,
and physically able to conform literally to what the several degrees respectively require of him."
The Committee was of the opinion that this did not violate the Ancient
Landmarks. (1900:865,868)
In 1914, the above rule, then contained in section 94 of the Constitution of
Grand Lodge, was modified by substituting the word "substantially" for the
word "literally" (l 914: 173); but it was held that substantial compliance
could not be obtained by use of artificial aids (1919:615), and further, that no
dispensation could be issued to avoid the rule. (1922:260)
In 1928, a Special Committee on Physical Qualifications, appointed to
conduct an in-depth study, reported to the Grand Lodge. This committee
proposed that the Lodges themselves should determine whether or not a candidate could substantially comply , and Grand Lodge then adopted an amendment
to the law by adding the following language:
''And the question as to the physical sufficiency of the candidate shall be
left to the sound discretion of the lodge. Where the candidate is unable to
comply literally with the physical requirements, the Master shall state the
nature and extent of his disabilities to the lodge before the ballot is taken ."
This is the present rule contained in section 512 of the C.M.C .
In 1931, Grand Master John Stewart Ross, author of the Ross Digest and an
eminent authority on Masonic law, decided that the Lodge must determine
whether or not the applicant is physically able to conform substantially to what
the several degrees require of him without the aid of an artifically substituted
hand or leg; that the ritual determines the question; and that Section 94 of the
Constitution must be read in connection with the ritual and as a construction
thereof; and that the amendment in 1928 in no way changed our law as to
physical requirements. He further stated that the results hoped for by the
amendment of 1928 had not been attained and recommended striking from
Section 94 the word "substantially" and also striking the provision leaving it to
the discretion of the lodge to determine whether a candidate could conform to the
ritual.
After reports from the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and
majority and minority reports from the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Grand
Lodge sustained the decision of the Grand Master, but did not amend the law in
any respect. ( 1931 :451, 725-731)
The next major attack on the rule was contained in resolutions in 1946. The
Committee on Policy and General Purposes, of which P.G.M. William Rhodes
Hervey was the Chairman, reported that from time immemorial the course of the
fraternity has been guided by certain unalterable landmarks, and among the
matters controlled by the landmarks was the matter of qualification of candidates;

As of 1971 when the report which has just been quoted was made, it was
reported that 42 Grand Jurisdictions of the 49 in the country permitted physically
handicapped to apply.
The Grand Treasurer of this Grand Lodge has requested of the several Grand
Jurisdictions their present law upon this subject. Each has replied relating the law
of that Jurisdiction. Your Committee has reviewed those replies and compared
the present law of each such Jurisdiction with the summary contained in the 1950
revision of the Masonic Service Association publication ''Doctrine of the Perfect
Youth." California and West Virginia retain the old rule. The other 47 jurisdictions have a variety of rules or interpretations which permit the receipt of
applications from persons who are maimed or have physical defects or deformities.
The points made on each side deserve the most serious consideration. It is
hoped that this recitation of the history of the requirements, the proposed changes
~nd past arguments will substantially lessen the time required for oral presentation by those on the respective sides.
There is one part of the proposal which deserves special consideration. The
last sentence of the proposed new Section 2603 (old Section 512.1) outlining the
manner of conferral of degrees upon physically handicapped provides as follows:

Committee has never been completely opposed to the relaxing of physical
qualifications, but rather that Resolution No. 17 is the first proposed change that,
in our opinion, contains all of the safeguards necessary to properly implement the
program.
This Resolution, as proposed, reiterates that initial action and control of a
person's qualifications is vested to the local Lodges. Every applicant must pass
the ballot box. The question of physical qualifications is relegated only to the
First Degree, as our present legislation directs that physical limitations do not
preclude the conferring of the remaining degrees.
The Committee recognizes the broad and impressive Masonic Spectrum
represented by the list of proposers to the Resolution. However, we hastily point
out that our judgement is based on the Resolution itself, and the same consideration would be given to a measure that contained fewer and less prominent
signatures.
Our Committee concedes, as perhaps other reporting Committees will, that
this legislation is not the perfect instrument, but with patience and preserverence
it can become a means of great good for our Fraternity.
The Committee on Ritual states unequivocally that should the Brethren of
Grand Lodge see fit to adopt this legislation, we are more than capable of
implementing it in the best interests of the Fraternity.
We enthusiastically recommend a "Yes" vote.

The word "represent" usually means to act for another. The implication here
is that the Master may appoint someone else to receive the work in the place of
the Candidate.
None of the 46 U.S. Grand Jurisdictions which replied to the Grand
Treasurer's inquiry by sending their applicable law have any such provision.
The assumption of conferral of degrees upon a Candidate himself is basic. An
applicant applies for them. The Lodge confers them. The ritual assumes the
presence of the Candidate. The conferral of our work upon a representative is a
departure from our age-old practice.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

RESOLVED that Section 2600 be amended to read as follows:
Section 2600 Moral and Physical Qualifications . An applicant for the degrees
of Masonry must be a man; no woman nor eunuch; free born; being neither a
slave nor the son of a bond woman; a believer in God and a future existence; of
moral conduct; capable of reading and writing; having no maim or defect in his
body which cannot be, or, if an understanding of the degrees requires
correction of the maim or defect, is not corrected by a prosthesis, corrective
aid, or other artificial substitute for the maim or defect, such as an artificial
leg, hearing aid, a speech aid, a brace , crutches and wheel chair, which will
render him capable of learning the art, and thus able to conform substantially
to what the several degrees respectively require of him.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 2602 be amended by inserting
after " requirements" in the fourth line " without the aid of a prosthesis or other
substitute for a maim or defect" and by adding at the end of said Section 2602
" In the case of defects not correctable with artificial or other corrective aids as
required by this code , the application shall not be voted upon by the Lodge
without the approval of the Grand Master.'' and by adding a new paragraph
reading as follows:
"If the physically handicapped be elected, the degrees shall be conferred upon
him in the manner provided in Section 2603 ."
With these proposed amendments, Section 2602 will read as follows:
Section 2602 Sound Discretion Required. The question as to the physical
sufficiency of the applicant shall be left to the sound discretion of the Lodge.
When the applicant is unable to comply literally with the physical requirements without the aid of a prosthesis or other substitute for a maim or defect,
the Master shall state the nature and extent of his disabilities to the Lodge
before ballot is taken. In the case of defects not correctable with artificial aids
as required by this Code, the application shall not be voted upon by the Lodge
without the approval of the Grand Master.
If the physically handicapped applicant be elected, the degrees shall be
conferred upon him in the manner provided in Section 2603.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 2603 be added to the California
Masonic Code to read as follows :
Section 2603 Conferral of Degrees upon Physically Handicapped Candidates .
The several degrees, without omission of any part of the ritual, shall be
conferred by the Lodge upon a physically handicapped applicant under the
supervision of the Inspector in accordance with guidelines prepared by the
Ritual Committee and approved by the Grand Master, and in such manner as
will preserve the solemnity , decorum and dignity of the occasion.
For the purpose of receiving the degrees the candidate shall be allowed to
wear or use the aid or aids usually worn or used by him , which shall be deemed
a part of his person of which he cannot be divested.
Where necessary, and if the candidate is otherwise eligible and is present,
another Brother who is qualified to do so may at the request of the Master
assist or represent the candidate.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 18 pertains to a request by Benicia Lodge No. 5 for the Grand
Lodge of California to forgive the sum of $5,000.00 owing the Grand Lodge as
the result of an original loan made to Benicia Lodge in the amount of $10,000.00
at an annual rate of 3% entered into the year 1972.
History on this matter reflects that a resolution requesting financing of
necessary repairs on the old Benicia Lodge Temple in an amount of $12,000.00
to $15,000.00 was made originally at the Annual Communication of 1971. The
majority of the Brethren at that time voted against the resolution. We add that the
disapproval was not due to any lack of merit of the project but rather was because
of the proposed means of financing the work.
At the 1972 Annual Communication a resolution was introduced requesting of
Grand Lodge a loan to Benicia Lodge not to exceed $13 ,000.00 with interest an
an annual rate of 3%, repayable at $100.00 per month, with said sum to be used
for the rehabilitation of the old Benicia Lodge building which is the first Masonic
Temple to have been built in California. The Committee on Policy and General
Purposes recommended a "Yes" vote, stating that there was no question as to
the necessity of preserving the building. The committee also stated that the
recommendation of approval was in no way intended to set a precedent for
similar future proposals for financing. The committee stated further at that time
that this project was of unique historical importance to Freemasonry in California
and that the urgent need for commencement of the restoration of the temple
building was worthy of support. This resolution was adopted.
Benicia Lodge has faithfully made the monthly payments of $100.00, plus 3%
interest, amounting to a total payment of $5, 133.09, including the October 1976
payment.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes remains in full agreement as
to the worthiness of the Benicia Temple restoration and preservation, and we
commend Benicia Lodge No. 5 for its faithfulness in debt retirement payments .
We also recognize the validity of Benicia Lodge ' s assertion that the Grand Lodge
of California should share in the cost of this total project.
However, the Grand Lodge, at the 1974 Annual Communication, established a
procedure by which Grand Lodge funds could become available for historical site

The Committee on Finance:
The Committee on Finance expressed its concurrance with the recommendations of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Not Adopted.

LEO E. ANDERSON, P.M., No. 355

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Some confusion seems to surround the decision rendered by Grand Master
Burton Meyer in regard to granting permission for members of Masonic Youth
Organizations (DeMolay, Rainbow for Girls, and Job's Daughters) to sell tickets
for Shrine Football games to the general public.
Grand Master Meyer correctly granted permission to members of these
organizations to sell such tickets to the public provided the activity had prior
approval of the Grand Lodge of California and the net proceeds thereof would go
directly to charity.
Grand Master Meyer's decision does not conflict with, and should not be
confused with, a prior decision by Grand Master Price which prohibited the sale
of Shrine Circus tickets by members of these youth organizations because of the
possibility of solicitation of the general public.
The two activities (football games approved by the Grand Lodge of California
and Shrine Circuses) are entirely different in intent and the funds produced serve
different purposes.
Activities such as approved football games whose net proceeds go directly to
charity do have participation by the general public, and youth organizations
should be permitted to participate therein in the same manner that they can sell
Christmas trees and other items to the public.

"The above Decision relates to a non-charitable activity where the proceeds
did not go to a charity as distinguished from Annotation 2070n which relates to
a charitable activity with the net proceeds going to a Masonic charity."

expenditure, one that will produce greatly improved personnel relations and have
included an item of $150,000 in the Capital Additions section of this year's
budget. (We move the approval of this action)

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

In compliance with our Code, the Grand Treasurer has presented to this
Communication audited financial statements for the fiscal year ending June 30,
1976. The auditors have indicated that the statements present fairly the financial
position of each entity of the Grand Lodge as of that date, and these statements
have been reproduced in the Grand Treasurer's report for your inspection and
review.
As you review the financial statements of the Grand Lodge, keep in mind that
your Committee on Finance recommended deficit spending last year, and that the
budget was approved accordingly. Our recommendation was related to our
continued effort not to overtax the Lodges.
The expenses of Grand Lodge increased 14.5% this last year; at the same time
the revenue declined 8.6%. Our budget proved reasonably accurate in the total
expense projection but was thrown out of balance substantially by an additional
net purchase of supplies for sale to the Lodges and an over-estimate of proceeds
from sales of our new C.M.C. There were some unexpected expenditures, such
as the $5,000.00 for the Malakoff Temple, for which no provisions had been
made, as well as a number of items which exceeded their original estimates; these
totalled $64,375.00, which includes the deficit of the California Freemason
Magazine, and were duly approved as supplemental appropriations by the Grand
Master. We recommend your approval of his action.
All of the above and much more comprise the bulk of the fine report of our
Grand Treasurer. As you read his report and realize the extent of his activities on
behalf of this Grand Lodge, you will share our keen appreciation of an
outstanding service he continues to render to this Grand Lodge. We move the
approval of the Grand Treasurer's report.
The financial support which you continue to evince with respect to our
Masonic Homes is extremely gratifying, especially in view of the costly

We call your attention to the fact that the proposed expense budget of
$545,900.00 reaches an all time high. Certain uncontrollable expenses continue
to escalate. As recently as two days ago we were informed that our Workrnens'
Compensation Insurance was going up a staggering 100% and that we could also
expect a substantial increase in the amount of our Public Liability Policy.
Although we budgeted for a deficit this past year, knowing that we had a few
years accumulated surplus in the bank, our 1976-77 prpposed budget produces
another sizeable deficit. We believe that it is now time to present a balanced
budget.

Investments:
Investments in securities purchased are carried at cost and
securities received by gift or bequest are carried at approximate market
value on the date received. Gains and losses are recorded when investments are sold. Investments are not written down to market unless a
permanent impairment in the value of such investments is considered to
have occurred.

Furniture, Equipment and Improvements:
Additions and betterments to property are capitalized at
cost and are not depreciated. Expenditures which represent maintenance
and repairs are charged to expense. The property accounts are relieved
of cost upon disposition.
Federal and State Income Taxes:
The Grand Lodge is exempt from federal and state income
taxes.

MARKET VALUE OF INVESTMENTS:
The portfolio of common stocks consists of investments in
sixteen different common stocks. Market value at June 30, 1976 for
fourteen of these investments exceeded cost by approximately $95,300,
The remainder of the account (38% of carrying value) has been invested
in two real estate investment trusts. Market value of these two
investments at June 30, 1976 was approximately $360,500 below cost.
Realization of the carrying value of these investments will be generally
dependent upon future economic conditions in the real estate industry.

Basis of Accounting:
The financial statements are presented on a modified cash
basis of accounting, Generally, revenues are recorded at the time
of receipt and expenses are recorded when paid,

NOTE 3:

PENSION PLAN:
The Grand Lodge contributes to the California Masonic
Retirement Plan for the benefit of all eligible full-time employees.
Total pension expense for the years ended June 30, 1976 and 1975 was
$10,365 and $8,486 respectively. All prior and current year service
costs have been funded. Assets held by the Plan at December 31,
1975 were in excess of vested benefits.

San Francisco, California
We have examined the accompanying statements of assets, liabilities
and fund balances arising from cash transactions of Masonic Homes of
California, a nonprofit corporation, including the permanent endowment,
property and restricted trust funds, as of June 30, 1976 and the related
statements of revenues and expenses and changes in fund balances for the year
then ended, Our examination was made in accordance with generally accepted
auditing standards, and accordingly included such tests of the accounting
records and such other auditing procedures as we considered necessary in
the circumstances. Other certified public accountants examined the financial
statements for the preceding year,
In our opinion, the aforementioned financial statements present
fairly the assets, liabilities and fund balances arising from cash transactions
of the Masonic Homes of California at June 30, 1976 and its revenues and
expenses and changes in fund balances for the year then ended on a basis
consistent with that of the preceding year.

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
JUNE 30, 1976 AND 1975

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

JUNE 30, 1976 AND 1975

NOTE 2:

NOTE 1:

The financial statements are stated on a modified cash basis
of accounting. Generally, revenues are recorded at the time of receipt
and expenses are recorded when paid, except that payroll costs are
recorded when incurred.
Investments:
Investments in securities purchased are carried at cost and
securities received by gift or bequest are carried at approximate
market value on the date received. Gains and losses are recorded when
investments are · sold. Investments are not written down to market
unless a permanent impairment in the value of such investments is
considered to have occurred.
Other Assets:
Other assets consist of life insurance policies, real estate,
and mineral rights assigned or bequeathed to the Masonic Homes. These
assets are recorded at the nominal value of $1 each for accountability.
Payments by the Masonic Homes of obligations of the assignors secured
by these assets are added to the nominal value, with the exception of
life insurance premiums which are charged to expense when paid.
Property:
Additions and betterments to property are capitalized at cost
and are not depreciated. Expenditures which represent maintenance and
repairs are charged to expense. The property accounts are relieved of
cost upon disposition.
Reserves for Special Purposes:
The trustees have established various special reserves to
which are added gifts and bequests and other amounts which generally are
used at the direction of the trustees for purposes other than direct
operating expenses, The assets represented by these reserves are included
in the assets of the General Fund,
Federal and State Income Taxes:
The Masonic Homes is a charitable organization exempt from
federal and state income taxes.

NOTES RECEIVABLE:
Notes receivable represent notes from sales of real estate
assigned to the Masonic Homes by residents of the Decoto Home and sales
of real estate received as gifts or bequests.

S'!ThMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:
Basis of Accounting:

287

NOTE 3:

RESTRICTIONS ON TRUST FUNDS:
John and Lena Luckenbach Fund:
The principal of this fund, restricted by the terms of the
will of the donor, is to be kept intact and the income used only for
the benefit of the care of orphans or the aged in Masonic Homes of
Southern California,
George F. and Laui:a E. Brigham Scholarship Fund:
The principal of this fund is held as a scholarship Fund for
the benefit of the Covina Home residents, of which $25,000 may be
loaned for this purpose. Income of this fund is restricted and may be
used only for providing scholarships.
Walter W. and Maude s. Schultz Scholarship Fund:
The income from this fund is restricted and may be used only
to provide financial assistance to needy children for educational
purposes.
Mildred R. Brown and Leroy G. Brown Memorial Fund:
Principal and income from this fund are to be used for making
loans for educational purposes to any children that the Board of Trustees
deem worthy.
Frederick E. and Frieda E. Somners Trust:
This fund is to be used exclusively for the education of
full orphan children.
George M. and Florence G. Perine Endowment Fund:
The principal of this fund, subject to the provision included
in the will of the donor shall be kept intact and only the income
therefrom shall be used for the benefit of the Decoto Home.
Harriet C. Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund:
This fund, in the original amount of $30,000 is subject to
a contract with the donor providing for the payments of certain life
annuities out of the principal and income thereof. Under the terms of
the contract, principal of the fund expended in payment of the annuities
is to be later restored out of income when the annuities no longer
absorb the entire income. After restoration of the principal to the
original sum of $30,000, the income from the fund is to be used for
the benefit of the residents of the Covina Home.

NOTE 3:

SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL INFORMATION

RESTRICTIONS ON TRUST FUNDS - Continued:
Student Aid Fund:
This fund is designated by the trustees for use for student
aid.
Edmund Clement Atkinson Fund:
The principal of this fund, subject to a provision in the
will of the donor, shall be used to contribute to the comfort, convenience,
and enjoyment of the residents of the Decoto Home.
Alida 0, Meserve Trust Fund:
The principal of this fund is to be used for playgrounds,
playground equipment, and other comparable fonns of recreation for the
boys at Covina.

The accompanyii:ig schedules included hereinafter, although not
necessary for a fair presentation of the assets, liabilities and fund
balances arising from cash transactions of Masonic Homes of California at
June 30, 1976 and the related revenues and expenses for the years then ended,
are presented as supplementary information. The schedules have been subjected
to the same auditing procedures applied in our examination of the financial
statements and are, in our opinion, presented fairly in all material respects
when considered in relation to the financial statements taken as a whole.
Schedules for the year ended June 30, 1975 were examined by other certified
public accountants.

Minnie E. Peterson Fund:
The principal of this fund is held by the Homes subject to a
life annuity.
Ralph Walter Kanz and Russell Joseph Kanz Trusts:
The principal and income of these trusts shall be used for
the education of the two named beneficiaries, subject to the discretion
of the trustees. When both beneficiaries have completed or abandoned
their education or reached age 27, the trust estate remaining shall be
distributed to the Masonic Homes of California.
The F,C, Hardy Memorial for Higher Practical Education:
The net income from this trust is to be used for higher
practical education.
The Roy G. Jones Trust Fund:
All income from this trust is to be paid to a beneficiary
for the duration of her life. Masonic Homes of California holds a 507.
remainder interest in the assets.
Santa Fe Masonic Club Fund:
Ninety percent of the income from this trust is to be distributed
to Covina <ltildren as cash gifts during the annual Christmas Party. The
remaining income is to be retained for fund growth.
NOTE 4:

289

PENSIONS:
The Masonic Homes contributes to the California Masonic
Retirement Plan for the benefit of substantially all full-time employees.
The total pension expense for the years ended June 30, 1976 and 1975 was
appro~imately $75,400 and $69,300 respectively. All prior and current
year costs have been funded. Assets held by the Retirement Plan at
December 31, 1975 were in excess of vested benefits.

balances arising from cash transactions of California Masonic Memorial
Temple, a nonprofit corporation, at June 30, 1976 and the related statement

in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards, and accordingly

public accountants examined the financial statements for the preceding year.
In our opinion, the aforementioned financial statements present
fairly the assets, liabilities and fund balances arising from cash transactions
of California Masonic Memorial Temple at June 30 1976 and its revenues and
expenses for the year then ended, on a basis consistent with the preceding
year.

Land, Buildings and Equipment:
Land, buildings and equipment are carried at cost and, except
for land, are depreciated on the straight-line method over estimated
useful lives of 50 years for Temple buildings and equipment, 20 years
for furnishings and 10 years for sound and lighting equipment. Maintenance and repairs of a minor nature are charged to expense when paid.
Betterments of a major nature, which extend the useful lives of the
land, buildings and equipment, are capitalized. On sale or retirement,
the cost and accumulated depreciation applicable thereto are eliminated
from the accounts and the difference between net book value and the
proceeds from sale or retirement is included in income,

were $173 in 1976 and $357 in 1975. All prior and current service
costs have been funded, Assets held by the Plan at December 31, 1975
were in excess of vested benefits.

STATEMENT
Masoni c Homes of California 's Pooled Income Fund is a trust
through which dono rs can make irrevocable gifts to the Masonic
Homes, retaining the income from the property for themselves
or for other living i n dividuals for life.
All contributio ns to the Pool are invested together, and a ll
life ben~fi ci aries receive income based on their proportion ate
shares of the Pool . Upon the death of the beneficiar ies the
gift is withdrawn from the Pool and is dis t r ibuted to Masonic
Homes of California , a charitable corporation .

A Pooled Income Fund gift is an irrevoc able transfer and affects

the donor's entire estate plan and current income situation. It
deserves the most careful considerati on. Donor s are urged to
consult their own a ttorneys before making Pooled Income Fund
gifts.

Masonic Homes of California 's Pooled Income Fund was establ i shed
a~ a t rust under California law on October 15, 1974 by a Declaration of Trust . The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes o f
California is the Trustee of the Pooled Income Fund and acts in
that capaci ty only so long as the Beneficiary or Beneficiari es
live.

To Board of Trustees
Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund
San Francisco, California

Income Fund, a charitabl e t rust, as of June 30 , 1976 and the related

a cco rdingl y included such tests of the accounting records and such other

In o~r opinion, the aforementio ned financial statements present
fairly the f inanc i al position o f the Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund at
June 30, 1976 and the income earned a nd di stributed for the year t hen
ended, in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.

the Pooled Income Fund and rel ated statement by Lindquist,
